“From the ashes of war, our people must rebuild. Our ancestors – sapien of The Fields, The Woods, and The Mountains – came together to create this grand kingdom. Let us not forget our history, let us not forget our tenacity – for our capacity to flourish in the face of change.”

–Queen Elise Arnur, during her coronation speech, 878 MK

                                                                                                    

 

Dotting every corner of the world, the sapien are by far the most spread and traveled of all of Ardor’s races. Tall, short, stout, thin with a diverse range of hair and skin colors, they are a colorful and diverse people that share many similarities with each other compared to other races. They bring with them a stout and hardy immunity and sheer determination to make any land home, and they have succeeded. They are firm believers of their own existence, and fight to make themselves known. Whether they are the aggressors or the aggressed, they persist despite all odds in ways that would make the fiercest loupain bow their head.

 

Like Others, Like Not

A dotting cornerstone of sapien is how similar they are to each other. This is apparent in both their nations and their individuals. Many sapien-led nations and tribes have faced fierce struggles for survival and have risen by overcoming oppression and aversity from land, beast and man. Their countries carry traditional and cultured histories and are often shaped by fervent faiths and philosophies. It is not hard to understand from this that the tenets and principles they frequently fight for is one part why sapien are ubiquitous worldwide.

Physically, sapien share many physical similarities with one another regardless of their place of origin – at least compared to those of other ancestries. It’s easy for loupain or agamidan to tell each other apart physically if they were from different lands. With sapien, the differences are subtler: skin color, hair, thickness of the lips, face and eye shape, and complexion among many others. Of course – it is offensive to say they all look alike! A sapien can easily tell, but it is also disrespectful to their diverse cultures and histories from their legacies on the world.

 

Sapien Across The World

            The ancestors of what are known as sapien today have spread and settled themselves in many continents across Ardor, surviving in different harsh climates to establish themselves. New Rogalia is a complex web of old and new conflicting with one another, having been stretched and wrought with political, religious or military direction; internal strife amongst external invasions by armies of the dead, Azoph-fer or Saint-Lorraine. To date, Rogalia still struggles to establish the kingdom it wishes to be to the rest of Ardor with two halves vying for control – now exemplified by their split with one half forming Weissel.

 

            The Mannish Kingdoms began as a set of island nations that have thrived in its solitude, until many nations have set their eyes on its natural resources. First came the Bahljetan traders and Luzunite speakers, then the supplanting Eirlanggan Dhusamati envoys, and finally the Rogalian colonists, each displacing the last as the native Mannish tribes and kingdoms shifted and changed over the centuries. At the last, the people unified and fought for revolution, claiming their independence as a people. The myriad of sapien nations of North and Southern Rodda itself was beset by Akai and Southern Zahnheim colonizers, which eventually had a similar tale of fighting for their own freedom and the right to reclaim their culture. From the Twin States of Barda to Noraki, all had bitter losses and sweet victories in the pursuit of their identity.

            These struggles are part and parcel in sapien history, but it does not necessarily make them a warlike people – it speaks to their passion and their desire to survive in the face of aversity, to carve an identity and place in history and a prosperous future for their kin. In times of peace, sapien strive to learn, build and grow their cultures and their technology, so that they may better themselves for the challenges of tomorrow.

 

From Settlers to Travelers

            Sapien easily settle anywhere and that’s in part due to their uncannily sturdy and hale bodies. Compared to other races they suffer fewer diseases or illnesses, and their bodies are well adjusted to many climates, which makes it easy for them to settle in just about anywhere or make use of many natural resources. Quite a few towns or even kingdoms started off as pastoral or farming villages located in the most unlikely places, and overall sapien have greatly influenced agriculture or means of cultivating natural resources.

            The traits and skills that they possess have made them great hunter-gatherers, and they have built entire cities from their propensity to draw from nature and sharing that bounty through trade. Their eye for harvest could have been why lands like Mann or Rodda were targets for other nations, as their unique spices or minerals were greatly sought after.

            Due to their pioneering and adaptive nature, having their origins coming from many different lands, sapien do not have a single, distinct culture that ties them together. They are the trendsetters of their own culture and traditions based on the nations they have founded akin to the loupain. Sapien who migrate to other nations tend to also follow in the footsteps of their new homes, a trait shared with lyncan, and they often bring with them reminders and cultural trappings that remind them of their ancestral home, like the agamidan. In this, they have made themselves comfortable settling anywhere in the world in the past and present.

Traits

Sapien

Humanoid

 

Sapien Lineages

Sapien ancestors originally came from three lineages. These lineages span back prior to the Meridae-Kirosis era, and even prior to the first eruption of Mt. Zaho. As a result, each of these lineages have inhabited most continents. While it is thought that most other ancestries’ ancestors have found niches that they have survived in with variable climates, the sapiens’ natural resistances and adaptability have allowed them to persist wherever their ancestors settled. These lineages are thought to be the result of these adaptations to their original biomes, and the forces of magic they interacted with the most.

Rogalia was one such region that exemplified these lineages the most. In its long history, the three lineages developed their own nations, and generations would be spent in opposition of one another before they began to seek unity. In Eirlangga, many of the desert farers were Piedan, though the jungles in Rodda were home to Liefen. In the mountaineous regions of the Pasiran, the Saltan inhabited the caverns alongside their eponymous, mountain-dwelling avekiri. Nature provided boundaries between these lineages, which in turn would result in fewer members of mixed lineages between the sapien of Eirlangga. Some sapien have sought to live underground, typically the Saltan of the Schattenriss.

Sapien of the modern day have settled themselves in many parts of Ardor. In Rogalia, centuries of unity had given cause for interlineage relationships to form, and as a result most sapien are usually of a mixed lineage. While some select traditions might view this as a desirable quality, it is rare that it is a prominent cornerstone of a sapien culture in the modern day.

 

Piedan

The piedan were sapien who lived in the grasslands, mesas and plains of the world. Remarkably long-legged compared to their peers, many of them had to have run for long distances to hunt or flee from large or fast creatures. Many piedan cultures are fairly migratory or have expansive, wide territory due to the sparseness and necessity for movement across flat plains and grasslands, and they have developed pastoral lifestyles to work the land.

 

Liefen

The liefen resided in the forests, coasts and jungles of the world, often shrouded in mystery and magic. With lithe figures and pointed ears, they carried a subtle grace while they weaved through woodland in silence or in tranquility with nature. Many liefen cultures drift in the direction of druidism or animism, and an affinity for the natural world.

 

Saltan

Short and stout, the saltan inhabit the mountains and canyons of Ardor. They’ve leaped across chasms and climbed up cliffs, making their living both outside and inside the earth. Their appearance belies their resourcefulness. The saltan of Ardor have an affinity for the air, the earth, and of fire. Many of their earliest cultures bear a religious or shamanistic slant rooted in the faith of spirits of these elements.

 

Sapien Heritages

Woodwalker Sapien Heritage

You grew up amongst sapien that have strongly adapted to life in the wood, knowing how to navigate it. You treat difficult terrain in woodlands as normal terrain, and you treat greater difficult terrain in woodlands as difficult terrain. You also gain a +1 circumstance bonus to Hide, Sneak or Balance in woodland.

 

Rockclimber Sapien Heritage

Your families lived by mountains and cliffsides. As a result, your community has a strong affinity for caverns and cliff walls. You gain a +2 circumstance bonus on rolls to Grab an Edge or Climb.

 

Plainstalker Sapien Heritage

You are a natural hunter, being taught by families growing up in lands of open prairie and valleys. You can make the most of tall grass and the rare trees for the purposes of travel and hunting, and these harsh lessons can teach you in journeys elsewhere. You become trained in Survival (or another skill if you were already trained in Survival), and gain the Terrain Expertise feat with Plains. You can use the circumstance bonus from Terrain Expertise for Stealth rolls.

 

Earthdelver Sapien Heritage

You grew up in communities nestled within caverns or underground, and this has taught you important skills to survive in the depths. You gain low-light vision, and you can reduce the DC for the flat check to target a creature concealed or hidden from you due to natural darkness by 2.

 

Mixedline Sapien Heritage

Your heritage is a mixed one, with a long line that merges families of other lineages and heritages. You gain the ability to select any sapien ancestry feat regardless of lineage or heritage requirements.

Special: If you are using the Golarion Ancestries rule, you can pick one of the following: Human, Elf or Dwarf; you can select any ancestry feats from the selected ancestry (at your GM’s discretion).

“So long as we live and breathe, we can strive for tomorrow. Let us stand strong, for we all possess fang and claw. Let your hearts sing with each beat and live! Under this four-fold banner, may all of Zahnheim be a home to all who cherish life and liberty!”

-Lord Ephram during the Four Swords coronation, 245 MK

 

 

The simplest way to describe the loupain is as a quadrupedal canine that has learned to stand upright. They’re the second most widespread of Ardor’s races, no doubt in part thanks to their natural instincts. ‘Survival’ is probably one of the most common words in loupain philosophical writing across history, no matter their geographical location. Like the quadruped ancestors they come from, they harbor strong loyalties and a desire for order – even if it is solely to their individual selves. Living is important; all else is secondary. This is evident in their customs, their crafts, and their laws.

 

Better Alive Than Dead

No matter where they come from, what their pedigree is, or the company they keep, being alive tends to be high on a loupain’s priority list. While this may be a controversial generalized statement (very few would contest being alive as a good thing), this does have some historical backing from loupain perspectives worldwide. Of course, the degree by which they value, interpret or ascribe to ‘living’ can vary.

For example, the Court of Magi of Kiel-Varron have often debated the philosophy behind being ‘alive’. One camp would say that life ends with the soul leaving the body. Means to prolonging this process defile that finality, and the undead are thus aberrations that need to be sent off to their permanent rest. Another camp argues it is more to do with sentience, and thus necromantic measures to extend one’s sentience – even if it meant living in undeath – would still be considered ‘alive’ and a valid means of survival. However, both camps agree that a lost soul remaining on the spiritual plane is a problem. This is a contrast to the once loupain-exclusive monastic Shepherd of Souls in Rodda. To the Shepherds, to be alive is to have purpose. Lost souls cannot move on as their purpose and wishes in life have not been granted. As such, monks are charged with the task of speaking and channeling lost souls by giving them their Final Purpose, and sending them to their next life.

 

Survival in Order

To a loupain, survival is better guaranteed when the order of things is known and kept. Change is only made when it is sensible or needed. Loyal by nature, loupain form strong bonds with what they consider important, such as their community, their family, or even themselves. In these relationships, there is often an established hierarchy; every person has their role and position. They tend to be protective of these bonds, and will not dismiss them without reason. This orderly and communal mindset is evident in most loupain communities, even in mixed-race communities where a loupain is a participant.

It would come to no surprise then that historically, loupain driven riots or rebellions are rare. However, this does not mean that conflicts of interest and protest do not happen; when they do, these conflicts escalate very strongly and very quickly. Loupain tend to view the world in terms of risks and potential benefits. The act of disrupting what is established as the best means of survival means that they have decided the benefits are worth the risk and are willing to accept the implications. As a result, all acts that bring chaos to an established order are often already thought out and not spur-of-the-moment.

 

Survival of the Fittest

By their nature of placing survival first, loupain are competitive. They are strongly driven to maintain their place in their circles, while also protecting the existence of the circle as a whole.  Loupain can be very resourceful or tenacious when it comes to maintaining the status quo. At best, preventing disruptions to the established order involves making sure that all possible threats realize that it simply is not worth the risk. At worst, it means the potential threats would need to be removed entirely.

Ambitious or driven loupain would be willing to climb up the social ladder if they feel that they are qualified or that it would lead to better stability – even at the cost of others. Depending on what’s at stake or what could be gained as a result of their actions, a loupain would be willing to take risks. 

Not all conflicts are a matter of life-or-death, however. On a general level, conflicts of facts, interest or opinion are seen as a challenge or a contest of some form. A loupe would deem it appropriate to try and come out on top to show that they are deserving of their place, or that they are capable of reaching greater heights. There are various means to achieve this, and context is crucial. Some loupes will choose to fight it out, while others will choose to debate. They can compete to settle their differences. Overall, however, the ends may not always justify the means. As long as the means do not risk too much, how a loupain justifies victory is on the conflicting parties.

                                        

The Lone Wolves

            Not all loupain require the order that loyalty to a company would bring. Sometimes, loupain do not fit. Other times, a bid for change has brought disastrous results. Perhaps the hierarchy has no place for them or kept them in the bottom with no opportunities to rise. While it is possible that they eventually find others to band together with and start anew, there are those who just remain distant from others or deny the natural calling until it no longer compels them. Popularized by the moniker of ‘lone wolf’, these loupain seek self-sufficiency. They are loyal to themselves or simply a few handfuls of old ties, and the best source of order in their own lives is to not rely on others at all. Trust is a commodity to them, and to be granted the trust of a lone wolf is rare.

            This isn’t to say they are necessarily recluses and are rare; on the contrary, lone wolves are not as uncommon as it may seem. They might live in cities and rely on the commodities that are offered by a town while working in community service. They could be loners who live in the woods and live off the land. While they are indeed stigmatized in some parts of the world – particularly among other loupain – they no longer find a sense of comfort or order in finding their place among the company they keep. Their goals are less likely to be the betterment of their pack, and more about keeping themselves alive and content.

Low-Light Vision

You can see in dim light as though it were bright light, so you ignore the concealed condition due to dim light.

 

Quadrupedal Limbs

Though you are primarily bipedal, your limb joints allow you to maintain a steady form. If you have both hands free, you increase your Speed to 30 feet as you run on all fours.

Loupain Lineages

The notion of a pedigree stems from all the way in the earliest days of the Zahnheimen Kingdoms era. However, it was a concept unique to the Zahnheimen loupain; purebred loupain are viewed as prestigious and honorable; while mixed-pedigrees – also called mutts – are frowned upon. History has not been kind to mutts, much like many other lineages that belonged to a fallen kingdom in the Zahnheimen Kingdoms war. They were relegated to the lowest rungs of society for so long, many had faded into obscurity.

However, in the eras following the Four Swords Rebellion the practice of discrimination by lineage was outlawed, and the notions of pedigree began to fade to history. In the modern day, most loupain refer to this concept as their lineage, tracing their origins throughout their family tree. While a majority of loupain ascribe to a dominant lineage and bear most of the qualities of their ancestors, those of a very mixed lineage get the best of all worlds, if not something unique to them and wear the title of mutt as a badge of honor.

In other nations of Ardor, while different lineages of loupain are acknowledged, it was rarely a cultural touch point in the same way. Some element of this could be because the loupain of the Zahnheimen Kingdoms are numerous and border each other where land was a constraint. On the continent of Freke or the lands of Akai, the borders of loupain lands are geographically or politically separated, whether it is due to mountains or deserts or a nation dominated by a different ancestry.

 

Special: If you are using the Golarion Ancestries rule, you can select any Shoony or Vlaka heritages and ancestry feats (at your GM’s discretion).

 

Garou

The oldest and the fiercest of the lineages, these wolf-like loupain are by far the strongest tied to their canine instincts. Some have ancestors who fled across the seas from the Akai shogunate; others come from forefathers who made the woods of Saint-Lorraine their home. Adaptable and loyal, they’ve settled themselves in many countries around the world. Garou loupain are commonly seen as soldiers, knights, clerics, and social workers – though any occupation that appeals to their nature of loyalty and community is a frequent candidate.

 

Bernardii

A large and strong lineage, the bernardii sport thick fur with sturdy frames. Originating in the frostbitten mountains and plains of Schneeberg, these loupes are naturally prepared for the cold. Bernardii tend to have a penchant for crafts and order, coming from centuries of Schneeberg building themselves as a conservative and trade-focused society. This does not leave them as unwilling to change or be challenged, however. Most breakthroughs in etheric metallurgy and masonry were credited to an eclectic bernardii craftsman, while a substantial part of Zahnheim’s oligarchical laws were based on the Mountain Kingdom’s. However, despite being rarely comfortable in warmer lands, some end up taking to tropical climes for the challenge or for the potential to hone new arts and crafts.

 

Schnauzen

The smallest of the major linenages, these loupes are energetic, curious and tenacious. Rarely breaking five feet in size, the bushy, wiry folk have historically used their strengths to their advantages as magicians, seafarers and traders. They originated in the seaside coasts that make up Meerhafen, and the various sunken ruins and islands surrounding the kingdom helped cement their skillsets in aggressively digging up and selling newfound relics. They say that there’s no corner of the world a schnauzen wouldn’t compete to explore and it shows. It is no surprise then that they are excitable or vocal, sometimes burning out into a bout of orneriness. Out of all the other lineages, they are indeed the most prone to disrupt order.

 

Selkes

With sleek coats, long drooping ears and a lithe frame, the selkes’ elegant appearance betrays the world where they came from. The grasslands and woodlands of Domus has always been a home rich in natural beauty, and its cities are ornate and built for prominent patrons of arts and music. Selkes loupain exhibit grace and culture, though they are not without their thorns. While not physically strong, they are naturally athletic. Their wit has demonstrated historically unparalleled levels of cunning and politicking in kingdom courts, as well. The selkes find themselves at home in the presence of society and culture. Undoubtedly, most well-known selkes loupain are artists, performers, bureaucrats, and visionaries.

 

Pinschen

The pinschen are a lineage of loupain who once held a kingdom between the lands of Schneeberg and Meerhafen. With most of their lineage being uniformly short black and rust-colored fur, pointed ears and a short tail, they bear a very cutting figure. As their kingdom dissolved in the Zahnheimen Kingdoms war, many of them spread across Eastern Zahnheim’s other kingdoms and found employ as hunters, trackers and mercenaries on account of their impressive sense of smell. Their kingdom’s dissolution was violent and sudden, leaving many scattered and without much of the way of their homeland or their culture. Exceedingly loyal as a people, these descendants have devoted themselves to the oligarchy for centuries and it is only recently that some pinschen have fought to try and reclaim their lost history and identity to stand apart from the other four main lineages of Zahnheim.

 

Frekian

Frekian hounds refer to loupain native to Freke. Generations of living in the arid savannahs of Noraki and the desert sands of Nobi have given most of them a range of short and black, blue or brown-shaded fur, pointed ears and snouts. The frekian have paws and digits best suited to traversing sandy or jungle terrain, and ears with sensitive hearing. Historically, they were hunters, priests and shaman of the wild lands, remaining apart from the native sapien or agamidan civilizations before their societies intertwined. They hold spirits and the thin line between material and spiritual planes in high regard, respecting the boundaries between life, death and spiritkind.  Subsequently, traditionalist Frekian have found their homes in many religious centers and neighborhoods, becoming prevalent and forming spiritual backbones as different faiths emerged and spread.

 

Zerdian

The Zerdian are the other prominent lineage of loupain that reside in the Nobi, extending southward into Rodda’s jungles and the Isles of Mann. In many instances, the Zerdian are characterized by their short stature and size, and disproportionately large pointed ears. Many Zerdian settlements featured a relationship close to the ground, close to underground reservoirs or building into caverns or cliff faces. However, the original Zerdian population has gone through tremendous upheaval through the movements of emerging nations and invaders of their settlements. As a result, many settlements were displaced or have been forced out of their traditional homes, typically on the Isles of Mann and the southern Nobi. Those that remained eventually assimilated to other nations over the many centuries ahead and many became of a mixed lineage that exemplify the loupain populations of tropical Ardor. The Zerdian that found their niches in South Rodda still hold strong to their identity and their old traditions.

 

Inuki

The Inuki are a lineage of loupain that are native to Akai. They are foxlike compared to the other native lineage of Garou. Historically, the inuki ancestors settled in woodlands and mountainous regions, becoming pioneers, herders and mediums who are well acquainted with the spirits who reside in these places. Unlike other lineages, however, they seem to have an innate talent for the forces of fortune and misfortune, said to have come from interactions the Inuki has had with deific forces in their homeland. As a result, it is said that each inuki is born with a curse or a blessing, determining if their lives bring misfortune or luck. As a result, many traditionalist inuki families are often very superstitious.

 

Loupain Heritages

Blackmoon Loupain Heritage

You and your families lived in areas of danger and fear, but have learned how to stand firm in the face of threats. Whenever you succeed in your roll against fear effects, you treat it as a critical success. Whenever you become frightened, you reduce its value by 1.

 

Pastoral Loupain Heritage

Your ancestors traversed great plains and survived its dangers, and their skills are still taught in your communities. You gain a +1 circumstance bonus to your checks to Tumble Through, and to your AC from attacks triggered by reactions when your mobility is not impaired through conditions such as being grabbed or restrained.

 

Dangersweep Loupain Heritage

You come from a line of loupain Dangersweeps, a historical term for shorter or more keen loupain able to crawl into dangerous places and delve deep into old ruins, often laced with traps and hazards. You gain a +1 circumstance bonus to detect and disable hazards and to your saving throws and DCs against their effects.

 

Frostforge Loupain Heritage

You are a descendant of loupain that lived in colder climes, and as a result you have a larger body with thicker fur. You gain a +2 circumstance bonus to your Fortitude DC or Reflex DC against attempts to Reposition, Shove or Trip you. This applies to saving throws against spells or effects that attempt a similar effect. If the Shove or Trip action fails and the initiating creature is one size larger than you or smaller, it is considered off-guard to you until the end of your next turn.

 

Sandhound Loupain Heritage

Your family consists of desert loupain, giving you more pointed-ears, shorter fur and limbs which are adapted to desert or humid climates. Sandy terrain is not considered difficult terrain for you, and when exploring these areas, you and any companions you travel with are not slowed by the terrain.   

 

Seadog Loupain Heritage

Your communities have an affinity with water, having swam in rivers or lakes or lived near oceans for generations. When you Swim, you increase the distance you move by an additional 5 feet and gain a +1 circumstance bonus to the check.

 

Pioneer Loupain Heritage

You grew up reading maps, stars, and the various signs that point you where you need to go, as well as the various tools and spells that can aid you. You gain a +2 circumstance bonus when using Sense Direction, and you learn the Know The Way cantrip as an innate spell.

 

Tombkeeper Loupain Heritage

Your community has kept sacred rites and watches over the dead and went over processions for births and deaths in your settlements. You gain the Stitch Flesh feat even if you don’t meet its prerequisites, and you gain the formula for Holy and Unholy water. You gain a +1 circumstance bonus to skill checks that pertain to handling the dead, such as Rituals, inspecting them, embalming them, or the like.

 

Mixedblood Loupain Heritage

Your family line contains many different pedigrees that have mixed throughout the generations, giving rise to a very unique blend of qualities that you and your direct family bears. You gain the Family of Mutts ancestry feat and one Loupain Lineage feat of your choice.

“I don’t believe it’s fair for me to talk about all lyncan’s experiences, but every single one I’ve met has reason to walk this earth. None of us are the same, but all of us are still so young. Because of that, we are treated like kits. But with no past to hold us, the future is of our own making. And I will never see a lyncan denied their future.”

-Zack Lightfang, Bane of Scourge, 876 MK

 

 

At some point in Ardor’s history shortly after the Awakening, chroniclers and scholars began to note something curious; felines were disappearing. Gone were the town’s local litters of cats, or the wild cats of the forest. Lions in Freke, tigers in the Isles of Mann, and cougars in Gere all became scarce. Around this time, upright, confused felines began to wander into towns. These are the lyncan – the first of Ardor’s magically evolved races.

 

A Different Tail, Worldwide

            The lyncan, or lynxan in historical texts, have had difficult lives. Unlike the vesperan, who were kept in their own little corner of Venteau, the lyncan were spread all over Ardor with little known explanation and cast into the world to fend for themselves. Some suspect a runic spell gone awry, but if true it is one of the earliest examples of transmogrification magic having permanent and ‘perfect’ effects. By all accounts, the lyncan are a fully-fledged sentient people that could reproduce and live as any other ancestry.

            Being creatures molded by magic, lyncan are well-tuned with ether, often possessing a natural aptitude for greater magical feats than the average person. More often than not, lyncan tend to be invokers. That said, when they first came to be, they suffered greatly; like the rest of Ardorean civilization after the Awakening, they could not control their magic. Worse still, no one had seen them before in the entire world. To different civilizations at the time, they were thought to pose some variant of threat, being thought of as invaders, ill omens, monsters or in one case, ‘savage creatures from the underworld’.

            For the lyncan, things would have to get worse before they would be accepted, for their history would be guided by the civilizations that took them in. In some lands such as the Isles of Mann and Rodda, the acceptance came quick once they realized the lyncan’s magical aptitude and their displaced nature, finding an opportunity to learn or make use of their talents. In Rogalia and Zahnheim, they were originally seen as invaders until they were noticed for what they possess. Even when accepted into their society, they had been viewed as inferior or as an other, often serving roles such as servants or magical tutors, before social upheaval gave them equal standing and the opportunity to hold positions of power, or the chance to escape and create holdings of their own. During the times of the Eirlanggan Empire, they were held as slaves, subjugated to dangerous tasks and experimentation before the old Empire was overthrown by the sacrifice of Horus – the first lyncan chimerian. Lyncan became free citizens in Eirlangga ever since under the new Sultanate, and now enjoy many freedoms that came with the Matriarch’s demise.

 

Painted by Magic

            With no strict heritage or origin, the lyncan follow the customs and norms of their home countries.  Of course, they have their own identity in the grand scheme of things; especially in regions where they were initially unaccepted. Lyncan find each other kin in some way or another – having been displaced or thrown into an unforgiving world to find their own sense of place – and thus they have historically found solace in each other’s’ presence, despite any differences.

There’s some truth to the stereotype that the lyncan are still cats – they are reserved or insular, preferring smaller groups rather than larger communities. They tend to form small pockets of lyncan neighborhoods in towns and cities, with knowledge of other nearby friendly or rival packs. Every now and then hackles raise between them, but otherwise these groups are tight-knit and look after each other both inside and out.

Being magically inclined has always given them a bit of a more ‘mystical’ standing among other races, and this could include myths about luck (good and bad) or the perception that they are all proficient casters and scholars. They have found a lot of success playing into this by becoming magical tutors, scholars or healers of all forms, and this could be attributed to their natural affinity with ether.

 

Resenting Their Past

Not all view the lyncan stereotypes as a positive, of course. Many lyncan resent them, equally so the lyncan who perpetuate it for their own gain. Lyncan warriors, craftsmen or civic servants find it hard to shake off that shadow in their line of work when others only see them as robe-and-hat types. Others find it much more of an affront, feeling that others only see them as a resource to exploit and have become distrusting of members of other races. In some cases, there are lyncan who are content to leave civilization and set up their own towns or villages as outsiders.

            These outsiders are met with varying degrees of success and acceptance. Some lands might allow them the freedom, finding that the outsiders that keep to themselves are fewer citizens to concern themselves with and could benefit the nation through trade. Others view them as criminals, who refuse to adhere to sovereignty – which becomes more complicated when some outsiders actively undermine regional authority. Further worse still is when outsiders face troubled times and turn to crime or desperate, darker means to preserve themselves.

            The most successful of these outsiders find themselves as well-situated and at peace with the local government, perhaps finding greater meaning to their ethertuned nature through study, worship or living away from the walls of cities and others who might take advantage of them. Being outside allows them the peace and freedom to greet others as equals rather than lesser.

            Many lyncan outsiders find themselves wandering if they do not settle. The Sangloup Nomads boast a large number of lyncan, some of whom bear forefathers that were part of the original Nomads who set out from Zahnheim.

            With lyncan taking the shapes of every kind of feline imaginable across the world, there are many physical differences between them, even though in the end their feline nature is consistent. Smilodon

Smilodon are the rarer, larger kind of lyncan – born from lions, tigers, and jaguar. They are physically imposing and built, with many bearing sharp sabretooths or manes that give them the appearance of apex predators. However, they have suffered the most with their transformation. Smilodon lyncan were far and few to begin with, and many perished in the aftermath of contact with civilization or an exile into the world. As a result, they are a scattered and small populace. It is a common thought amongst smilodon that they are a dying kind; smilodon populations that remain have a strong sense of self-preservation and will to live, and often seek the means to stay that way. They share a mutual respect for loupain in that regard for their drive to survive. Today, if they do not find themselves as outsiders, they are usually renowned warriors or generals due to their physical prowess and survival instincts – a worthwhile, well-paying risk that can offer a good degree of protection and respect for their family and their kind.

 

Wyldian

Wyldian are more commonly found compared to their sabretoothed brethren – born from lynxes, servals, leopards and cougars. Smaller and communal, they lean much more heavily on their magical gifts, natural wits and agility. They can be found in almost every country, having adapted themselves to their hosts; in fact, most citizens of Ardor think of Wyldian when they think of lyncan. As widespread as they are and having reached some level of acceptance in various places, they can be found working in every vocation; most will think and actually find of them as mages or scouts in some form or another but there are lyncan lords or retainers in countries that allow them to hold authority such as Zahnheim, Rodda or Akai.

 

Hearthcats

Hearthcats resemble domesticated cats who have lived near or in civilization, possessing one of the smaller builds compared to other kinds of lyncan. Their lack of physical robustness is made up through their versatility. Many hearthcats have historically found themselves becoming civil servants, merchants and agricultural workers; however, most notable lyncan in history have been hearthcats who set out to prove themselves equal to other lyncan, seeking a life of adventure or glory through sheer determination and use of their gifted talents. Their general attitude and disarming appearance give them much more flexibility in cohabiting in settlements with other ancestries, and because domesticated felines are common in all of Ardor, they can be found worldwide.

 

Fenin

Fenin lyncan are amongst the smallest of all lyncan, born from the smallest feline predators in the wild. They have short statures with flat faces and shorter ears, typically with a rotund or wiry appearance. Depending on their origins, they might possess a large amount of fur or lack thereof and have an impressive capability to regulate their own body temperatures and understand the temperature fluctuations in their surroundings. As a result of this natural gift, most Fenin populations can be found in temperature extremes such as the frigid peaks of the Pasiran mountains, the taigas of Akai or the desert regions of the Nobi. As a people, their short stature does lead to less physically taxing positions, but their gifts have actually served them in roles of being civil engineers and architects, pioneering a surprising number of practices in the developmental field of construction.

 

The Fenin lyncan were once derogatorily seen as physically inferior or more cowardly to larger lyncan in some instances, but that could not be farther from the truth. In many situations, the fenin lyncan have fought tirelessly for the rights for all lyncan, and no effort is more visible than in the War of the Small, where they actively fought not only for their right to avoid subjugation and slavery, but to push for more freedoms amongst the lyncan populace on the continent of Freke during Matriarch Yiazma’s rule during that era.

“Let us be where we please, for we are older than thee.

From our clutches where we came, we hold our legacy all the same.

They live within us in spirit and blood, and their grace is like a flood.”

-Old Proverbs and Poems, “Like a Flood”, 400~ MK

 

 

The agamidan are best described as cold-blooded reptilian humanoids. From their substantially smaller, twitchier ancestors, they possess a unique form of homeostasis that lets them adapt to vastly different environments to stay in top shape. A ‘cold-scale’ can sit in the tundra and not feel the bitter chill of the weather, while a ‘sand-scale’ can traverse the desert with little trouble in the burning heat. This adaptability is the most striking feature that they have, and yet they have been slow to spread across Ardor. Perhaps this has to do with the strong ties the agamidan have with their ancestors and traditions; among the known ancestries of Ardor the agamidan are steadfast in retaining the memory and ways of their foremothers. While their origins are a far-flung memory for agamid society, the original six clans have defined much of how agamids are today. They are of many shapes, sizes and colors; from bulky and angular to small and lithe, from frills and horns to spines and fins, the agamids trace a storied history of family and land, from egg to adulthood.

 

Life Under Scales

            Simply put, the agamidan body is built to let them live wherever they would like, but in a different way than a similarly adaptable ancestry like the sapien. If the sapien thrive worldwide because their bodies are resilient against foreign environments and disease, the agamidan thrive in many places in Ardor because their bodies can fit any climate well. As they’re exposed to newer climes, their bodies begin to adjust their functions in such a way that greatly favors the new climate. Some of these changes are physical, such as new scales being grown possessing a different layer of thickness or colour, and some are biological, where natural heart rates will accommodate to the level of heat the bodies need. These changes require compensation in an agamidan’s day to day, such as adjusting how much they might need to drink, what type of activities are desireable, or how much exposure to sunlight they need to help their bodies regulate. While inconvenient, some may say it’s a fair price to pay to be able to thrive in harsh environments that would normally give pause to other races.

The agamidan’s oldest ancestors originate from the Nobi Desert, on the northern half of the continent of Freke. From the onset, the agamidan are no strangers to threatening climates, as the region has high temperature extremes and is dry. The desert lands face pools of hot air trapped by the Marajan Mountains, while the crags can reach freezing temperatures. Plants and water are a rarity in the harsh terrain.

            Outside of the purposes of trade, the agamidan have been slow to spread across Ardor. Those that crossed the desert southward have found themselves in Rodda, among the grassy wetlands and marshlands; others that crossed the sea to the west settled in the Isles of Mann and their tropical jungles while sailing the ocean northward landed them in the icy fjords of untamed Saljund; and finally, those displaced in the Runic War found themselves at the base of the Holy Mountain of Enara, and never returned. There are individuals who have travelled and settled in faraway lands; but curiously the agamidan have never truly settled far and wide the way the sapien have.

 

Traditions Across Borders

            Before there was the Sultanate of Eirlangga, before the Awakening brought magic to all races, there were the Six Clans, spread across the Marajan Mountains and the Nobi Desert. The First Matriarch, Yiazma the Elder formed the Eirlanggan Empire by uniting all the clans across the desert under the auspices of Dhusamat, the Golden Light. Under her rule, these clans still possessed a strong sense of identity and tradition, retaining their teachings and customs with the grace of the Majelis Al-Dhusamat even as centuries passed. Though the agamidan were not ones to easily change, the truth of the matter is that they have kept the parts of their culture that they could keep and changed what they could not. This is as true for modern day Eirlanggans as those who have moved to another nation and assimilated with them, even those who worship different gods.

            Undoubtedly, most Agamidan are protective of their traditions and their possessions, for they have a strong sense of honouring boundaries. While they are welcoming of outsiders in general, their expectations can cause friction. It tends to be the case that an agamidan will welcome you to have tea and show you their home, but they expect that you understand that family rooms – the equivalent of a living-room part in an agamidan home where the family would have dinner and leisure are strictly off-limits unless invited. Or in other cases, an agamidan guest would prefer to not be seen without their familial shroud or clan ornaments in public when they are invited to a gathering.

While it can be difficult to accommodate for, there is an evident sense of respect and understanding between guests and hosts, and once understood this often plays into all parties’ favour in getting along. An agamidan will value their host’s wishes, and this is true for all cases – whether its social callings or cultural expectations. If the demand crosses a line, then the agamidan will simply step away or leave.

 

Unity in Ancestry

Most modern-day agamidan trace their lineages to their original clans, and possess a sense of reverence for their predecessors of eld. As their ancestors have lived and died, they continue to live on inside their descendants. It is not unheard of for agamidan families to have a small shrine in their home dedicated to their ancestors, or perhaps a more recent relative who has passed but performed great deeds in their life. In other cases, folk heroes or sages are revered in a similar way, and this creates a collective dedication to those who have enriched their lives.

This connection fosters an especially strong kinship for agamidan regardless of their clans. For this reason, it’s common to see agamidan quarters or neighborhoods in cities outside Eirlangga – there is a distinct interest among agamidan to be with others of the same kind, as they seem to have exceptional common ground even though they have never met due to their ancestors whether it is through blood, clan or by deed.

Most agamidan who have ties to Eirlangga or the Nobian nations typically worship Dhusamat or Sada’ahmar, and the millennia of dhusamati or ahmarite teachings inform how they view the afterlife and the dead. In their texts, there is often reference to the final rest of a soul that moves on, whereupon they await for their descendants to join them as they convey their wishes for them from the beyond.

Because of this reverence, there is a code applied to the souls of the dead who await their final rest. To physically and mortally perish is to cross a line that should not be walked back from. As a result, many forms of necromancy are frowned upon to traditional agamidan clan teachings. The dead should stay dead, and how one chooses to extend their lives is a complicated subject altogether. Agamidan are no strangers to long-lived rulers, but there’s are good and wrong ways to achieve this. Communing with the dead, banishing a restless soul, or guiding them for a purpose that encourages them to plunge into their final rest are fine in various contexts, but raising the dead is taboo.

 

Pariahs Across The Land

Despite the implications of agamidan being so tightly wound to their ancestors and their traditions, they are not bound to them. By nature of their physiology forcing them to change and adapt slowly, or centuries of traditions and honor being upheld in their society, it can be difficult to push away the communal weight of expectations. Some agamidan refuse to be tied to or follow the footsteps of ancestors long dead. These pariahs range from those who shun or ignore the expectations of their honor-bound kin or those who simply want to live their lives without thinking of their customs, even if they still follow most of them out of habit or simple pragmatism.

In the eyes of other agamids, those who shirk their clan or familial ties consists of agamidan who are better off on their own or outcasts that do not belong to the lineage altogether. In fairness, it is a very thick line to cross – in most situations, agamids are accepting of variations or conflicting views in practicing their culture – especially those who live in foreign lands. After all, agamidan are capable of acclimating to the land, and this can translate to social circles; not all changes need to be the same. One might even be able to argue that these pariahs are still following their nature of making changes as they go through life – even if it is more drastic than the a clan traditionalist would like.

There is an expression among many Eirlanggans – ‘adder-born’, often hissed at outcasts. It is a degrading insult among all agamids that has a history that dates back to the days of the Eirlanggan Empire. Amongst the six original clans, one clan known as the Night Adders had never accepted the First Matriarch Yiazma’s Eirlanggan empire ever since it was formed. They tirelessly undermined her rule and Dhusamat’s teachings, and the changes it has brought to the clans. Further still, the Night Adders grew wealthy from the grave crime of fostering the trade of slaves. Eventually, the Matriarch decimated their clan by sending one of her Immortal Guard to sink their famed cities into the desert’s depths. As the years passed, the Night Adders faded to small obscurity and those born to the clan face prejudice to this day amongst the extreme traditionalists, though some cling on to vengeance as a motive to destroy the modern day Eirlanggan Sultanate.

 

 

Six Clans, Six Scales

            After centuries of coexistence, the six clans still remain important to traditionalist agamidan families, who still prefer to maintain their individual cultural identities. Each clan is affiliated with the lineage of an agamidan, with physiological differences and approaches to magic steeped in their own traditions. Even though at the surface level some elements of an agamidan’s physiology changes through their adaptation, general physical traits and features such as frills, fins, horns and tail shapes are strongly affiliated with their ancestral clan.

Despite this, many agamidan have begun families that stretch and mingle across various clans, and their children bear a mixture of their parents’ qualities, typically favoring their mother. As a result, there are agamids of many colours and many sizes, owing to both their lineage and their environment – and many agamidan are proud to show it. Strolling down the markets of Bhajar, you can find clan or familial ornaments such as rings adorning frills, or piercings on fins, or coiled up spines among agamids large and small with every colour imaginable. This explosion of expression is half the reason agamidan markets are so sought after for travellers and sightseers.

            The theme of ‘environmental influences’ continues even into their reproduction. Agamidan have a lifespan of about 120 years. A mother can lay one or two eggs at most, where the egg will sit for about half a month in development. During this time, certain factors (especially temperature) can change qualities of the developing whelp – scales, colour, size and most importantly their sex. Historically this has had great influence on agamid society, where agamid towns may have hatcheries (similar to the avekiri) or even a dedicated room in homes to make sure the eggs have an environment that will keep the developing young safe and healthy. Control of these hatcheries was historically important to birth controlling programs to determine the birth of male or female sexed agamidan, though as populations flourished it has become less critical to control. It’s been thought that this was why historical agamidan culture was much more matriarchal, as mothers were often charged with tending to the eggs.

Agamidan Lineages

In the modern day, the agamidan concept of lineage is strongly affiliated to the clan an individual traces their bloodline from. In the centuries that followed after the end of the old Eirlanggan Empire to form the Eirlanggan Sultanate, clan traditionalists have eventually settled in various territories and nations within Ardor, giving rise to a concept of a homeland for the clan itself. Even if members of a clan have since moved away, they usually have some affiliation to distant families of the clan that remain.

Gilded Scale

Those of the Gilded Scale bear vibrant scales, with wide ranges available to them than any other ancestry. This clan in particular originates in the northern ranges of the Marajan Mountains, and eventually formed the Empire of Eirlangga after their Matriarch, Yiazma the Elder, united all the other agamidan clans under their one banner. Their vibrant scales and adaptive physiques have historically made them natural envoys and diplomats. Some even have very striking crests upon their head that is seen as a mark of royalty or prosperity. Their culture is strongly affiliated with Dhusamat’s teachings, with one of unity and outreach to bolster a community, and to lead by example.

 

Salted Frill

The Salted Frill occupied the coasts of Northern Freke, once occupying territory that spanned south from Herki and into modern day Perigia. Those of this clan bear wide frills around their neck and fin-like protrusions along their limbs. They bear wider, longer footprints that allowed them to inhabit settlements designed with water and regulated flooding within coastal caverns. These affinities allowed the Salted Frill to dominate as the Empire’s navy. Their traditions hold fast to the lessons of the ocean: to move with the tides and to cherish and preserve the communal sources of nourishment and bounty.

 

Scarlet Feathers

The Scarlet Feathers clan are agamidan who inhabited the lands of Noraki to the northeast of Freke. Many were ardent worshippers of Sada’ahmar, known to them as Orazec in the local dialect. Once, the Eirlanggan Empire spanned to their savannahs and jungles, and the Scarlet Feather held the empire’s territory for the centuries prior to their fall. Their feathered plumes and winged flaps granted them a degree of mobility amongst the trees of the jungle and their stony strongholds. Their culture is that of oneness with nature under Dhusamat’s light, to live well each day as each one is a blessing.

 

Ember Horn

The Ember Horn clan are known for their physical prowess and mastery of the desert sands. Their bones are substantially more powerful to withstand their greater muscle mass. Many bear sharp spines and horns, while others have powerful jaws that can destroy bone. Their clan worked the land and became masters of glass and metal for the Empire, and they have a culture of excellence that is emphasized in each newly hatched child. Dhusamat’s teachings have impressed upon them to apply themselves in everything they do, for every person has a role in their community.

 

Venom Tongue

The Venom Tongue clan lived closer the Palmer’s Coast, on the southern ends of the Nobi Desert. They clan consisted of more portly shaped agamidan who reside by wetlands and oases, with larger jowls and longer tails compared to other clans. In the Empire, the Venom Tongue was specifically known for their alchemists, who had a wide variety of ingredients due to the location of their settlements, along with one key element: their potent saliva, which was known at the time as a miracle solvent for its powerful, versatile properties. It can be used as a deadly poison, or it could be turned into a powerful remedy. Some say that this was enabled by an engorged and magical salivary gland that has a symbiotic interaction with animacules and spirits. While medical studies have only recently delved into this in detail, such a quality was known to the Venom Tongue clan early in their traditions, where they have always understood the fine line between cure and poison and the value of patience when doing all things – be it cooking, hunting or brewing, especially when it came to using their saliva as an ingredient.

 

Night Adder

The Night Adder clan have thinner and wiry frames compared to other agamidan, with very distinct colored tongues that change with their scales. They have an uncanny ability to adapt far better than their peers, some of which can change the color of their scales temporarily to match that of their surroundings. For much of the clan’s earliest history, the Night Adder lived in unprosperous territory that required substantial investments in magic and agriculture to develop. They eventually were driven strongly for Dhusamat’s edicts to pursue prosperity, which lead to the Muddharim family to eventually overtake much of the clan and their territory’s wealth. However, the eventual downfall of the Night Adder and the destruction of their lands had scattered them, and many of the Night Adder’s descendants occasionally face scrutiny at worst, or empathy at best, from other agamidan, for their ancestor’s transgressions still are etched amongst traditional agamidan.

Cold Scales Agamidan Heritage

Your heritage features agamidan who have lived in deserts all their life, surviving under high temperatures. You gain fire resistance equal to half your level, and treat environmental heat effects as if it was one step less extreme. Your Acclimator terrain includes deserts and dry regions.

 

Toxic Scales Agamidan Heritage

Your families reside close to jungles and wastes, where fumes and toxins are prevalent. As a result, your scales and your blood become resistant to such threats. You gain poison resistance equal to half your level. Whenever you need to make a saving throw against poisons, you treat the outcome of the roll as one degree of success greater. Your Acclimator terrain includes wastelands and jungles, or similar areas where poison is prevalent.

 

Earthen Scales Agamidan Heritage

You live amongst agamidan who inhabit the earth, and your body has adjusted to take after the qualities of soil and sand, retaining mud, sand and dirt that grounds you and acts as a natural barrier to disease. You gain electricity resistance equal to half your level. Whenever you need to make a saving throw against disease, you treat the outcome of the roll as one degree of success greater. Your Acclimator terrain includes caverns and underground locations.

 

Benthic Scales Agamidan Heritage

Your body is accustomed to being inundated in water, and your scales are excellent at repelling liquids. You gain acid resistance equal to half your level. You are not considered off-guard while you are underwater without a swim speed and gain a +1 circumstance bonus to your Swim checks. If you have a swim speed, this bonus increases to +2. Your Acclimator terrain includes riverlands, seasides and swamps.

 

Teratoa Agamidan Heritage

You come from a community who reveres the great turtles of the world, and don great shells to wear once you have come of age. These shells are built specifically for the agamidan that is meant to wear them, and you’re have undergone the training needed to wear them in all occasions, as expected of you.

 

You gain a Teratoa Shell that you can wear as body armor.  A Teratoa Shell is heavy armor in the Plate group and grants an AC bonus of +5, a Dexterity cap of +1, a check penalty of -3, a speed penalty of -10 feet, and strength requirement of +3. Because your shell is specifically designed for you and you have trained to use it, while wearing it you use the highest armor proficiency you have (including unarmored), and you add the Comfort and Flexible traits to your shell. While rare, if you need to remove the armor it takes ten minutes. Losing or being forced to surrender a Teratoa Shell is a taboo amongst your people.

 

Stillheart Agamidan Heritage

When you were an egg, you had a brief moment where your heart lay still; the strange lack of rhythm had knock-on effects after your hatching. You do not adapt as strongly as agamidan, but your heart is able to withstand moments of time where it does not pulse and you do not breathe. You gain the Diehard feat. Whenever you would die from when your dying condition, roll a DC 18 flat check. On a success, you do not die. Instead, you stabilize and reduce your dying condition to 1 value below where it would. Each time you succeed, you increase the DC of this check by 1 for 1 week. If the DC would increase beyond 20, you die the next time you need to make this check.

“Rest here in our mountains: Rahm’s wings shield all of Enara and our songs echo the crags. Be embraced in His light, and welcome His wind. For here, we are safe, and here, we are free.”

In the mountains of Enara and Pasiran, birdsong echo from tower to tower, some several dozen kilometers apart. The song is carried as it bounces across peak to peak. At each tower, a songmaiden sits, listening. As she hears it, she stands and sings her next verse; her voice flowing through the wind to the next tower. And as it reaches the next tower, another songmaiden continues the verse, As the holy songs continue, the mountains are kept protected.

 

Birds of Song and Spirit

The avekiri, (once known as the Aileseau by Domish colonists) are avian humanoids who, by virtue of their bone structure and home, have grown reliant on magic for their basic needs. In eons past, the avekiri broke free of their drachiri masters with the assistance of the Great Beast Rahm, and have settled themselves under his guidance in the mountains of Enara. Two of their five Flocks have left northward towards the crags and mountains of Freke, while the remainder have lived in the Holy Kingdom ever since.

The three flocks in Enara revere Rahm, offering themselves in service of the avian spirit through spell and song, inviting all who came to their land to join in their worship. Enara has only recently allowed travel and study abroad, and eye the outside world with suspicion and caution after having lived under Rahm’s protection. Meanwhile, the avekiri of Freke who did not settle in Eirlangga or Rodda lived in seclusion in harmony with the land, pursuing magical or philosophical goals. Over time, some have eventually departed their homelands in a similar fashion to their Enaran counterparts to share their learnings and teachings.

Some avekiri pride themselves on their magical ability, some to the point of becoming antagonistic to the magically-evolved lyncan and vesperan ancestries; they view the two as having been granted their aptitude for magic without having spent the centuries of training the way the avekiri have.

 

A Life with Purpose

            Avekiri prefer stability in their life, often seeking to make sense of their place in the greater scheme of things. Each of the Enaran flocks could be thought of as one of three parts to the progression of their holy kingdom, with each flock’s members having well-understood and defined roles in service to Rahm and Enara. In the Pasiran Mountains, the peregrin have espoused similar ideals in their mountain tribes, with each possessing specific duties to empower their collective whole. For the strigid of Cordova, they organize themselves into schools that fixate on particular branches and avenues of learning. Even avekiri in other lands follow this mindset, performing their roles and tasks at home or at work with due diligence and pride.

            It’s not a mistake to say this is a long-standing habit with history behind it; when they served the violet dragons, avekiri were similarly (perhaps even more strongly) segregated by their flock for each of their strengths. When the violet dragons vanished, giving the avekiri a few moments of freedom, they scrambled to find someone that could unify and lead them when they feared the drachiri’s reprisal. When Rahm appeared to guide them, the avekiri followed him and remained within their flocks, playing to each of their specialties throughout the War of the Wings. After Rahm’s First Flight, the drachiri fled, defeated – and the birdfolk were now truly free. With Rahm returning to the spiritual plane, the Holy Kingdom dedicated to his worship was founded. In order to never lose sight of their savior, the avekiri have found solace in structuring their people by their flock, each playing a role in protecting the people Rahm had come to save. In the end, it was the promise of certainty and stability that kept them unified and that still holds to this day.

 

Birds of a Feather

            Community is one of the defining features of the avekiri culture. As a very communal people, avekiri prefer to keep their company strong. The needs of others outweigh their own, and thus they strive to maintain their harmony and well-being. This is regardless of any single flock that they belong to; there is often an espoused and acknowledged set of layers in a community that grows outward. For Enaran avekiri it includes their family, then their flock, then Enarans as a whole. For the Pasiran and the Strigid, it covers their family, their tribe, all tribes, and all living and spiritual beings of the mountain. This concept, when understood in concert drive the decisions that individual avekiri make.

            This is not easily known to most outsiders, primarily due to the contentious history avekiri has had with other races. They have been slower to accept other races, for one reason or another – but most primarily is the perceived threat to the harmony and unity to the avekiri way. If all avekiri think of their lives and communities in terms of their flock, then they all would come to similar conclusions, or at least similar intentions. However, other races might not be as understanding – and thus, distrust grows.

            Of course, there is no perfection in the avekiri’s way; there are not only individual pariahs within these flocks, but it is arguable that whole communities have been shaped due to this mistrust. In Enara itself, living on the holy mountain is reserved for those who have achieved greatness and closeness to Rahm. While pilgrimage is frequent in the theocracy, which includes traveling to the eight towers of the mountains and the holy city of Avinar, being granted the permission to live in the mountains is rarer. For those who have yet to meet those goals, they are considered Wingless – and thus they must live at the base of the mountain. Here, avekiri, azoph-fer and agamids live together – perhaps in what could be considered a flock of their own – but are viewed as less trustworthy or holy compared to those who live on the mountain.

The avekiri’s language, Navarren has historically been a language that can only been spoken by others of the race and well-trained Vesperan due to the vocal cords that only they possess. To accommodate those who have arrived on their shores and their kingdom, and those avekiri who travel, Navarren has been split into two: Ravarren consists of the avekiri specific sounds, and is meant to be spoken by avekiri who have been granted the right to reside in the mountains and for worship, while Navarren itself is meant for all others.

For avekiri such as the Peregrin or Strigid, and those who have settled outside the walls of Enara, this tale takes a different turn. Unity and cohesion is expected, but an individual ends up becoming far more invested in prevailing customs and preferences. Debate does become more common, and some even have grown to welcome the variety in thought to challenge their own. Their reluctance to diverge substantially from common approaches and thoughts does make them come off as stubborn, however. That said, impractical or frivolous senses of superiority – such as wealth, status symbols, or even the use of Navarren as a language rather than Ravarren over accolades, knowledge and qualifications becomes far less common.

 

A Path to Greater Things

            Ambition is a newer concept to avekiri. In Enara, while they may have their share of leaders now it was all too recent when the race had been kept docile by the drachiri. The violet dragons weren’t overthrown by rebellion – they had vanished without a trace. Rahm appeared in their hour of need and protected them, guiding them to victory in the War of the Wings, and then returned to the spiritual plane. The communities of Strigid and Peregrin avekiri have rarely thought of a status hierarchy, typically preferring shallow or distributed leadership traditionally through councils, a single elder, or communal, early forms of parliament. The improvement and survival of the whole has been a tremendous consideration for so long for them, that the notion of managing larger populations and strata of leadership or rank has only come to the fold once their civilizations have settled and grown.

            With the absence of true figureheads, their freedom has been a journey to understand their newfound agency, and with it, the pursuit to become greater. More avekiri have felt compelled to achieve this in some form; often seeking to become better spiritually or physically, gain more accolades, or travel farther than their peers.

            Such lofty pursuits come with their own share of risks. Sometimes this goal clashes with the intent on preserving their peace, or that it necessitates inviting external forces into their fold, such as outsiders – and its results have become points of contention. Ambitious avekiri are welcomed with a degree of caution, for the end results could benefit the whole or bring trouble.

 

Flightless Wings

Avekiri, having originated from birds possess brittle, thinner bones. However, due to their size they are unable to naturally fly as one might expect, but some are trained to be able to glide and slowly descend by use of their fairly sizable wings. As they have evolved, avekiri wings have evolved to curve and curl along points towards the ends, giving them the ability to grasp things in their wings as if they were hands. While it can be somewhat clumsy and dangerous, the ability to hold things with more limbs than just their talons or beaks has given avekiri the capabilities of any other sentient race in handwork.

Magic plays a large role in their way of life. Construction of avekiri infrastructure often requires the assistance of spells to compensate for the fact they are no longer small nor natively flight-capable birds; the power to fly or carry materials into the air become especially important in constructing the towers and perches that avekiri are fond of. With weaker bones than most other races, combat is frequently dangerous so travel and gathering is often accompanied by liberal use of spells.

Due to their circumstances and preferences, Avekiri homes and towns are often perched higher in the air. Space is a rare commodity when living on mountain lands. Saltan sapien have circumvented this fact by building into their mountains and caves, but avekiri decided to build their homes upwards. Their buildings often utilize plenty of stairways and ladders to help them climb up, and perches of various sizes to denote ‘rooms’ even if it is all within a single tower. Hatcheries tend to be a communal building in villages, kept safe and secure by being higher above most other buildings where eggs are kept safe and cared for until they hatch, but sometimes avekiri parents would prefer their eggs be kept at home, instead. Larger buildings tend to be a series of connected towers, with bridges spanning their length. Very few places would be close to ground level, usually reserved for public or very large grounds such as marketplaces, prayer grounds or monasteries.
