In the western lowlands of Venteau, the Ivory dragons found themselves seeking a powerful weapon to combat the drachiri’s enemies, the avekiri and their deity, the great beast Rahm. Using their boundless intellect fueled by curiosity, they transformed the local bats into a new race of upright, intelligent beasts who would share the ivory dragon’s traits: curious, impartial and possessing a very strong tie to magic. Centuries later the vesperan race had split away from the drachiri and their loyalists, establishing a kingdom of their own where the ivory dragons once ruled. Celebrating pursuits of magical sciences and death in all its forms, the vesperan would leave a mark on all of Ardor.

 

A Darker Calling

            To most ardoreans – even where people are accustomed to their presence – vesperan are considered strange. Weird, morbid, or even immoral are some of the choice words that people use to describe them. There’s a grain of truth to that, but it comes with the baggage of a lot of misconceptions.

            Vesperan love the cycle of life and death, there is no mistaking that. In Murciel, the kingdom built from the ashes of the ivory dragon’s domain, each coming of a new season comes with the celebration of the dead and buried and those who have yet to join them.  During these festivals, people say hello and goodbye to those fallen, and pray that death meets those living in the best circumstances possible, with a fulfilling life lived.

            In Murciel, the second most common school of magic is necromancy. Now, while uncommon, most ardoreans are fine with a controlled measure of magic that controls life and death. There’s also something to be said of a mystical offshoot dedicated entirely to seeing and speaking to the dead, too. Clergymen, gravekeepers and other magical healers frequently agree to the practice. But what’s the most common school? Blood magic. This is where the rumours and wariness fly. The vesperan have created and perfected this art of controlling a creature’s flow of blood, helped by the fact that most vesperan are reavers, but the notion – and the potential – is a line crossed too far by folk.

            But there lies the wellspring of misconception. The vesperan push the boundaries of magic, being less caring for societal standards when it comes to discovery and study. And it is true – vesperan have changed the face of magical warfare throughout the world, having created some utterly devastating and terrifying wizardry. However, there is plenty that Murcielans hold sacred that can be said true of most vesperan.

 

 

 

Stradling The Moral Line

            Vesperan care for the important cycles of life and death, about as much as the freedom of individual pursuit. But then where does the line sit, for a race dedicated to delving deeper and deeper into the possibilities of magic?

            It is a line that vesperan governance still struggles with to maintain. After all, they had broken free from their draconian masters to establish their own land and freedom – so why should they be held down when they are capable of greater things? Even so, vesperan have sought to keep their progress steady and in check.

Contrary to notorious belief, law-abiding vesperan do not have their own private armies of the dead, let alone a single relative brought back to life. In Murciel, it is forbidden to forcefully resurrect a dead sentient creature, except in times of great need, as the dead – who wish to stay dead – should be granted that rest. However, undead pets or familiars are more acceptable. On a similar vein, moral vesperan do not have blood puppets or blood banks in their basement. The usage of blood magic to willingly restrain, exploit and torture is by and large outlawed. However, there are many who want to put themselves forward in the pursuit of magical advancement – sometimes with little regard to their well-being or laws. In Murciel, there are many laws and safeguards in place to ensure that such a drive doesn’t cause harm, but that poses its own lines of trouble. At the end of the day, the fervent scholars of blood want to take their risks, while the world has already painted them as disturbed creations of dragons.

 

A Cloud Over Ardor

            Despite these perceptions, vesperan have been welcomed or accepted in many places across Ardor. Their knowledge of spellcraft and dedication to the art has been a blessing to the progress of medicine, biology and aetherology worldwide. Pick up any recent study of sapien anatomy and it is likely that a vesperan is cited. Tinctures for common headaches were first invented by a bat. The Foundations of Arcana – a mainstay of any magical academy – was co-written by Dario Cadanza de Chira, famed Murcielan scholar.

            The kingdom of Murciel sees its diverse share of history, being the land the vesperan first called home. When the great beast Rahm defeated the drachiri, the bats rebelled against their creators, declaring the land theirs. With little power remaining, the drachiri retreated into the mountains or scattered across the world. Some loyalists followed their masters into the Gorge and left the newly found kingdom to pick up the pieces. Finding an ample share of death and magic in the wake of Rahm’s destruction, the vesperan saw to it that no magical resource was wasted while they built Murciel. Now, they are prosperous and spread across the western third of Venteau, meeting with their departed ancestors with each new season in celebration.

            Some twenty years after their freedom (around 64 MK), the vesperan encountered Meerhafen explorers wandering into their shores. These explorers traded and offered their assistance in building Murciel in exchange for their expertise in magic. Both kingdoms benefitted greatly, and this began the close relationship between Murciel and Meerhafen – and later, all Zahnheim. For their help in the century following, Saint-Lorraine granted them their own dukedom, Flederheim, and vesperan have lived across the entire oligarchy since. They are still considered eccentric or morbid by some, even for the well-touted canine roughness across the kingdom, but they have accepted the bats due to their shared history.

            Beyond Zahnheim, vesperan have taken root everywhere – some with mixed success. The Murcielan approaches and customs find little purchase in Eirlangga and Rodda, where necromancy and the lengths vesperan are willing to go for knowledge are frowned upon. They have found some common ground with the Mannish and the Rogalians, with their people appreciating their contributions to magic and medicine. Many apothecaries or magical schools are run or assisted by vesperan, and while there is a very concerned and watchful eye of their practices, the average citizen’s health has only improved. Even so, people who can look past the parts that may disturb or go against their own beliefs of how the dead should be handled can easily see that the vesperan have genuine respect for the departed in their own way, even if to them death is not necessarily the end to a family member.

 

The Price of Progress

            Some vesperan dub it the Ivory Curse; an effect of the white dragon’s influence in creating the vesperan race. There is a strong push in vesperan nature to dive deeper into their pursuits, sometimes with little regard for the cost – not unlike a member of the Ivory brood. However, it is substantially less pronounced in the bats than it is in the dragons, and it isn’t enabled by their trademark apathy. Indeed, vesperan are much more passionate in their crafts; but there are many that still find the necessary laws and stipulations of morals and ethics chafing.

            While loyalists followed their masters into the Gorge, there are still vesperan of Murciel who saw fit to continue the dangerous experiments that were started by Ivory or Verdant dragons. Necromancers raise their corpses in secret, ritualists forcefully bind spirits to their will, while blood mages prey on volunteers’ willingness to give themselves for dark sciences and magics. These are indeed criminals by Murciel laws, but the unspoken outcomes have bled into the wealth of knowledge that benefits Ardor to this day.

            These vesperan find their criminal status well worth the gains and live in hiding as they continue their studies, while others have simply turned to more nefarious or selfish purposes. In Murciel, there is the frequent danger of warlock and witch covens, which delve deeply into dangerous practices and seek to actively fight back against Murciel and their laws. Worse still are the influences or ties they may have to the Drachiri Empire remnants – posing a serious threat to the kingdom’s safety. These covens practice very powerful and debilitating magic that cripple, transform and dominate their victims, frequently using the most potent and dangerous forms of Blood Magic. To combat this, Murciel has formed the Hexhunters – a force dedicated to combat covens and root them out, utilizing the powers that the kingdom itself has banned.

 

Wings Without Flaps

            The vesperan body is well defined from their original roots as common bats found in Venteau and neighboring islands; With thinner legs and leathery wings that span the length of their upper body, most common articles of clothing worn by other races are tough fits as they have no sleeves to speak of. They are not adapted to carrying heavy weights, with legs as thin as theirs, and most of their clothing are loose, flowing ponchos or capes that drape over their torsos, with some elaborate armored scales or chain ponchos becoming common among the more martial types. Out of necessity, most vesperan are trained with the knowledge of how to sew, tailor or alter other races’ clothing to accommodate their inability to wear sleeved clothing. The vesperan are able to grip and hold onto things by fingers that extend at the end of their wings, which allows them to perform many of the same functions most sentient races are able to do with regards to handwork. Many vesperan are also able to grip and hold onto things with their feet, as well.

            Vesperan are unable to fly, similar to their avekiri counterparts; however, like the birds they are able to train themselves to glide, and frequently utilize the art of spellcraft to grant them the ability for flight. Their architecture, originally based off of their former ivory dragon masters feature spacious single room spaces with high ceilings and secluded nooks for privacy or storage. Open spaces are thought to be better at inviting ancestors into their homes, with comfortable arches and tiny corners for them to rest alongside their descendants. Their buildings are also quite angled in some respects, with sharp, pointed protrusions to curl around or sit – or even to let other feral bats come to rest.

Every child is filled with stories of them; the mere mention of their name is enough to invoke fright as if they crept in wait, ready to snatch them if they were misbehaving. Hobgoblins come to steal you in the night. Bauchan corrupt and ruin the trees. The Servants of Devils turning you to blasphemy. Bloodthirsty fiends intent on rending children limb from limb. Blood drinkers, leaving your corpse to dry. The list goes on. In the times since, they’ve become known, but suspicion and trust are always a coin toss away. The memory of grisly drawings of misshapen flesh and horns during war; the old tales of violent rituals and sacrificed prisoners; the sight of ferocity and rage as blood rained. There is a story behind the legends, but their truths are scattered and its roots are secluded in the most dangerous lands known to man – the Isle of Zaho.

 

A Bond of God, Earth and Beyond

It’s important to understand the bond azoph-fer have with their creator to comprehend their origins. According to their legends, the deity Azoph-met mixed his own blood and ribs with ash and fire; and from the ashes rose the Azoph-fer. He instructed his first children in his ways and the goal of bringing Eternal Balance. Each step of the way, he sacrificed more of his physical form to strengthen his children, empowering them and enlightening them for the task that lay before them. When there was nothing of him left, Azoph-met departed Ardor for 'The Realms Beyond', where he lies in wait for the day he is resurrected – and returned, he has.

Azoph-met, the Lord of Blood and Cosmic Balance was once said to be the last remaining descendent of Bapho-met, among his 32 other siblings. In the year 924 MK, most of his siblings returned to Ardor, pursuing Azoph-met back to the fiendish Hells and the land of Zaho. Azoph-met pursues Bapho-met's desire to bring Cosmic Balance', the complete details of which are known to only the top few of the Azoph clergy. According to the azophites of Zaho, the cosmic order of the universe violently shifts between flux and stagnation. If left in its imbalanced state, existence would begin to fall apart tear itself asunder. As such, Azoph-met’s teachings implore his followers to reign or unleash the universe by any means until a perfect state of balanced flux is reached.

To the Azophites in Zaho and abroad, this is achieved by the Eternal Strife – an eternal war that has been fought amongst the Azoph-fer kingdoms that is political, spiritual and violent, spanning both material and spiritual planes with waxing and waning states for the past millennia. Though the origins of the Eternal Strife are often contested, at the core of this conflict is the historic rivalry Azoph-met and his siblings have with each other, seeking conflict and subjugation of land and dominions in Ardor and Espiria, and with every victory and defeat, their symbiotic influences become apparent across the continent.

Originating from Zaho and Azoph-met himself, the azoph-fer are amongst the strongest tied to this conflict and their creator’s goals, even though they may have drifted away from azophism and generations passed, typically landing into the worship of his other siblings. But in some respects, the bond with their creator is absolute and inescapable. Some element of their lives comes back to Azoph-met: A family heirloom carved from the first azoph-fer’s bones, passed down to the warriors of their lineage; secrets that must never be uttered to outsiders in fear of courting curses; or the myth that their souls will return to Azoph-met upon death, to be reborn anew within the Strife. It doesn’t matter if they’ve left Zaho, their kingdom or their faith – even generations down, there’s always that tie to that connects them to Azoph-met and his own personal domain within the Hells.

In the end, this bond can exemplify itself amongst the occasional newborn azoph-fer. Colloquially known as the helltouched, the ilzanarii feel this connection more strongly than their kin, manifesting in a substantial drive to achieve and accomplish something with their lives. At best, this leads to them pushing themselves and driving them to do great things, but at worst it manifests in a restlessness or ambition that falls into dangerous lines. The ilzanarii can tap into more primeval powers affiliated with their creator, and many are sought after or fall prey to the tempting promises of power and success by followers of one of the Bapho-met siblings, being born or influenced to become a cazic-fer. Powerful leaders and diplomats, or warlords and killers are made from the ilzanarii who feel and listen to their desires far more than their kin, and some say this has to do with a perpetually lengthening line of lives returning to be born anew by their creator Azoph-met. It is celebrated in some azoph-fer communities as a sign of greatness, but for those who want to distance themselves from the Eternal Strife, it can be seen as a curse.

 

A Land of War and Blood

The azoph-fer are one of the oldest known races in Ardor. They originated in Zaho, a massive, danger-fraught continent with a massive eponymous volcano. In Zaho, there are many Zahoan Kingdoms, each with their own goals that typically lay in conflict with each other. Many worship or adhere to one or more of the children of Bapho-met, while a few are more pragmatic and accepting of their place in Ardor, and want to establish their might to their rival kingdoms and elsewhere in Ardor. One might pursue Azoph-met's goal of bringing Cosmic Balance', while others fight against his goals under the banner of another deity. Their differences and conflicts feed into the Eternal Strife which ultimately serves to maintain a constant push and pull between order and chaos within Zaho. Though bloody and destructive, it largely keeps the Strife strongly on the continent they call home.

That said, some of these conflicts spill elsewhere in Ardor. With the return of the siblings to the world, the conflicts have expanded. Where the rivalries cannot be met on the fields of Zaho or the hellish domains prominent in their regions, some azoph-fer take to other continents to proselytize or take root in outlying lands, doing the bidding of a sibling’s interests. These actions have painted a most difficult picture for azoph-fer who have fled the conditions of Zaho to try and find a life away from the din and siren song of the Eternal Strife.

Some point to the azoph-fer as the reasons why entire villages have bought the rhetorics muttered by an azoph-fer page of a child of Bapho-met, or why Zahoan raiding ships have pillaged towns for goods and people to take back to their kingdom, and it has given pause to small communities of azoph-fer who had escaped their conflict from pushing their luck in formally integrating with others. Even if their communities were not the sort to shut their walls or attack other ancestries on sight, the azoph-fer face being shunned, hated, under suspicion, or are sworn (or cursed) to secrecy from others.

Most curiously, however is that being as old as the Zahoan Kingdoms are, many of their oldest texts, regions and figures bear the titles implying or glorifying heresy, and others openly mock or blaspheme against ancient deities and orders, particularly those affiliated with the Holy Planes, which begs the question of what came prior to faith in the 33 siblings.

Spirits of all types play a large role in Zaho: some are permanently bound, others willingly serve the sibling or siblings they follow, while the rest are much more fickle or primal. Most participate in the Eternal Strife in some fashion, passively or actively. With the nature of the conflict, the spiritual plane itself is in itself a battlefield; azoph-fer frequently not only fight in the material lands, but also inside the spiritual plane as well. By and large, the greater spirits of Zaho fall under the umbrella of being fiends or associated with a domain located within the Hells. The boundaries between the two planes are thin, with many spirits having shaped and influenced both lands in their own ways – the spiritual lands span from fearful hellish landscapes of fire and brimstone to cold, decayed lands.

 

Renouncing Land and Lord

            There are azoph-fer who have left Zaho for one reason or another. Some find the rigid militaristic aspects of their kingdom too chafing, or perhaps they were thrown out for treason or from some political move; others may have decided to renounce their worship of Azoph-met or another sibling and escaped to avoid the death sentence. These azoph-fer have found homes in the fringes of Ardor with varying degrees of success.

Most notable are the azoph-fer who became servants of the drachiri in Venteau, prior to the destruction of the dragon kingdom. Since the dragons’ departure, they have lived in relative peace with other Earthdwellers at the feet of Enara’s holy mountains. It is unheard of for them to be allowed into the mountains or holy cities proper, being met with more hostility and suspicion than any other Earthdweller. They are otherwise at more ease than they have been in Zaho, having called the valleys home for generations. These azoph-fer have long forgotten azophism most of its practices, having adopted worship of Rahm in its place. Some azoph-fer instead worship dragons in secret -- though the act of dragon worship is an act currently punishable by death in Enara.

            On the Isles of Mann, after having been constantly under threat or siege throughout Rogalian or Eirlanggan colonization, the local azoph-fer have secured the island of Simedang as their rightful land as part of the revolution that earned the Isles their freedom. Here, they practice a form of shamanism and animism derived from their local and zahoan roots in peace. Their tribe have fought for the independence of the Isles of Mann, with some evoking their ancient powers at risk of expulsion to secure victory.

            Elsewhere, the azoph-fer are relegated to the corners of continents. Azoph-fer are seen dubiously at best or hunted down at worst in most of Ardor’s nations, with generations of fairy tales or historical recounting of invasions and Zahoan pillagers or proselytizers having terrorized or razed lands causing them to be painted as dangerous monsters. Those who are able to build a society find it difficult to be part of more than a small village in unwatched or uncivilized territory. Others who are braver or more desperate find employ as mercenaries, or become brigands or even clan adventurers, all of which are either groups made up of society’s pariahs or those who look past their race and history.

            Not all azoph-fer seek refuge, of course; some prefer to continue their practice of azophism unfettered by their kingdom’s rigid rules and structure, and see nothing wrong with the rites and sacrifices necessary to bring the Cosmic Balance. Through these azoph-fer, azophism has taken root in various parts of Ardor, attracting people from all races to join in the pursuit of a lord dedicated to tilting the cosmic order.

In the depths of untouched and untamed wilds by riverside forests or seaside glaciers, one might find the Pinotr, the apprentices of the giants of ice and the tides. Though few giants remain and fewer still remember their lutrine allies, the Pinotr still carry and build upon their taught and earned traditions. From their small tribes and communes they hunt and release magic back into the earth and the sea. Stewards in many ways, simple in others; the pinotr have only just recently began to truly interface with the world that is far larger than they could ever have been taught.

 

Webbed Wonders

The Pinotr are a race of lutrine sea and river-dwelling humanoids, resembling otters or seals in appearance that have kept to the temperate and arctic seas and riverlands of Ardor. They have webbed hindpaws with a fin-like forearm. As an aquatic ancestry that spends a good portion of their time on land evolving in arctic climes, they have numerous adaptations that assist them in life on both land and sea.

Their webbed hindpaws allow them to traverse land and to propel themselves in water. Meanwhile, their fin-like forearms, dubbed a seolaf (pronounced sho-laf), have a series of fin-like arrangement of bones connected to a hinge. The resulting appendage allows the pinotr to rotate the seolaf laterally on a hinge bone and allows it to flap, curl or shift inward or outward, forming a grasping appendage that can fold backward to allow fin-like mobility as needed, allowing it propel the pinotr through water. The seolaf structure is encased in a firm layer of muscle and flapped hide to sustain these motions, though it creates this almost ‘long-sleeve-like’ appearance for their arms.

Like the aquatic mammals they resemble, their fur varies in their length between being short or plush, with some having thicker layers of blubber that keeps their bodies insulated, despite the arctic chill of the lands they hailed from. Whether they emphasize one form of insulation over the other, typically comes down to which region of Ardor their families hailed from.

 

Hunters of the Frozen Wilds

Equally at home in land and at sea, the pinotr’s history began in small nation-tribes that have deep traditions of hunting great beasts of magic. These nation-tribes are mostly found in the northern continent of Saljund, and stretch to series of island forests further south that approach the Ardorean mainland or eastward towards Noraki. The great beasts they hunt bear an extraordinary amount of accumulated ether, and sometimes reach tipping points where they become apex predators or even begin to overthrow the domains of spirits of their habitats. For these, the pinotr tribes would send their hunters to fight on land and sea, whereupon a successful hunt would release its bountiful gift, which then nourishes and sustains their homelands while the balance of the ecosystem is rebuilt anew.

As a people, they have often remained insular, though they are rarely hostile to those who respect their lands. Over the course of centuries, however, conflicts have risen as nations expanded and their sights were set on many resources that remained untapped. The bountiful, ever-evolving nature of the lands the pinotr have hunted in for generations bring unique, flourishing changes with each felled great beast, and such a thing is a tempting prize for enterprising nations wanting to acquire magically aspected materials.

Often, these conflicts have resulted in great deals of skirmishes and hostile invasions, and a greater effort by the nation-tribes to remain vigilant and hostile to outsiders. However, they often find allies in the form of druidic circles and ecologists who wish to study or keep the phenomenon of these environmental cyclings untouched.

Some tribes are appreciative of the assistance, and maintain cordial and comfortable relations with those who value their lands, while others remain skeptical or outright insistent that their lands are not meant to be trod upon by those who were not nourished by it. A part of this skepticism is cultural, due to the fact that some nation-tribes see themselves as stewards who had been offered the land by their ancient companions, the giants, and they could not relent until their return.

 

Primal Stewards

 The pinotr tabulate and transcribe their history upon bone, rock and leather that is worked through imagery and art that are imbued by runecraft signatures. In their historical transcripts and paintings, they describe that their people had acquired stewardship over their tribal lands from the people who once held them – the giants. In a prominent piece from the Tarkarikul tribe, they drew ‘The Departure’, where their stewards bid the pinotr to stay upon their homelands, and traveled into the ocean and sunk into its depths, where they never returned. Since then, the pinotr have taken it upon themselves to mind their land and ensure that any time anything would threaten the sanctity of their homeland, they would rise to protect it.

The pinotr have been known to wield magic for about as long as every other ancestry on Ardor, and they attribute this knowledge to their giant stewards. Their familiarity with these magics are historically supported by the fact that giants were known to wield primal elemental powers and runecraft prior to the Awakening, and though it has evolved and changed since, the style of magic they display bear strong resemblances to archaeological findings of giant runecraft. That said, even though their knowledge of magic is presented in primal druidism, they display a great understanding of the flows of magic in a way arcanists would. The movements of leylines and stellar patterns of ethereal currents are thoroughly detailed in their writings, some artistically depicted in both similar and eye-opening ways that bring new perspectives into magical academia.

 

Ancient Letterings

To many outside looking in, their runecrafting bears familiarities to the techniques developed by spellsmith cultures around the world, which lends itself to the ideas that the art of using runes is knowledge that came from an era prior to the awakening. While functionally similar, the pinotr have never used this knowledge for the purposes of warfare – at most, these runes are etched onto their weapons that are best suited for their hunts. Even if certain nation-tribes are hostile or bear arms against each other, they have sworn off use of runic weaponry in these conflicts.

Instead, a large majority of their runecraft goes onto their pelts and bone. It is an important rite of passage for a Pinotr to know how to inscribe runes onto another’s pelt, as a form of community and trust, if not to inscribe onto bone-made accessories after successful hunts. These are believed to heighten their power and act as a mark of growth, giving them the courage and strength needed to take on greater hunts.

Even despite all this, the pinotr have only the most basic understanding of the runes, seeing them as symbols that depict an important aspect or element ascribed by the letter used – not unlike spellsmiths and engineers who utilize runes in their day-to-day-work. Very few have the grasp of stringing letters in way that a runic magus would, as oftentimes in their culture each runic letter or word is sacred and besmirching this ancient knowledge by carelessly using the runes has often lead to punishment or disaster.

The fact that their nation-tribes are aware of and use runes have not escaped the notice of international runic councils of Ardor dedicated to stave off and enforce harsh limits on the application of the Runic language. In the wake of the Runic Wars, there have been more focused efforts to convince or coerce the pinotr nation-tribes to adhere to internationally held standards, which has seen limited success. To the critics of runic councils they would often point to the Pinotr as strong reasons why such limitations should be done and away with, while those who are proponents of runic limitations frequently scheme to find ways how the pinotr could be convinced, if not to find ways to incorporate or adjust international standards to accommodate for limited applications in the ways the pinotr have.

 

A Magnetic Understanding

A common phenomenon amongst the pinotr is an uncanny familiarity and understanding of where True North lies. They have a surprising aptitude for direction, and such a talent is immensely helpful as they navigate hunting grounds to find their quarry. Some historical writings depict that the giants had blessed them with the knowledge of finding the northernmost star where their greatest hunt lies, though physiologists have discovered that the pinotr have enhanced organs in their inner ears that seem particularly receptive to a northward direction like an inner compass.

This northward affinity is a shared element amongst all pinotr, but it becomes particularly exaggerated as more runes dot their pelts. Many pinotr who are well decorated begin to have vivid desires to ‘return north’, to their ancestral homelands of Saljund, as something drives them. This is partly one reason why most Pinotr are found in the frozen tundras of Saljund, and for those who inhabit other regions bear strong cultural interests in getting more powerful and decorate themselves in runes before embarking on their greatest journey.

Of course, no Saljund landmark is currently more known than the Delve of Ibirian, which many pinotr have taken as their ultimate destination. Some think it too coincidental to ignore, while others feel that their true great and final hunt lies somewhere in the most inhospitable remote ice plains of Saljund. Regardless, many pinotr who embark on this journey never return. Even so, the Delve of Ibirian acts as a swansong for many, and the pinotr are not alone, where the nation tribe of Sak’i’jaran created an eponymous town around the massive chasm and have partnered with Eirlangga and Rogalia to manage the immense influx of pinotr hunters, arcanists, occultists, and adventurers who wish to comb its depths.

 

Stewards Worldwide

            While the pinotr have been and are reclusive in their nation-tribes, preferring to maintain and curate the homes left to them by the giants, not all tribes are equal in their seclusion. Some interface with the outside world more readily than others, either due to geographical proximity or due to the evolution of relationships over the course of centuries. Some coexist better than others, but ultimately it leads to trade, a shift in culture and technology, and political relations.

            Some pinotr closer to the coasts of Noraki or Northern Gere and Freke have enjoyed a wealth of trade and influx of newer technologies, which then ultimately seeded itself to all but the most secluded or traditional of nation-tribes. Many had to fight or bleed for their right to independence, and some had sought to conquer these lands the way they had colonized Rodda or the Isles of Mann, but such efforts were strongly hampered by what the pinotr called ‘The Elder’s Wrath’, where the great beasts of the land often end up attacking and destroying massive landmass developments. To the pinotr, their lands are wild and not ones to be conquered – and they fight to reclaim the magic in their great hunts for the land, and to repel would-be threats that could ruin a carefully balanced ecosystem forever.

            This attitude is pervasive amongst these nation-tribes, and as the centuries passed, stewardship and the cultural process of growing up in these lands to eventually become great hunters or leaders, and potentially leaving for the north or to become their homeland’s defenders is what some people have only known. But like many things, change would come. With the stories and arrangements from the outside world connecting to the pinotr and the growth of the nation-tribes over time, one of three things happen. First, it becomes more likely that the influences irrevocably change the local culture and approach to their tasks, where their duty of stewardship begins to take a backseat. Second, the growth leads to the land becoming less sustainable for the population of pinotr in their own homelands where beast attacks become more of a concern. And last, the youth begin to seek something different from all that they are expected.

            For some pinotr, these were signs for them to try and find their living elsewhere, where they could raise their young or find their fortunes outside the confines of their traditional lives as stewards of their giant-granted lands. But this does not stop them from remaining vigilant and attentive to the needs of their community and their environment, no matter where they settle. Indeed, the pinotr are a communal and social people – as a result, they are often helpful and hardworking, and many of them typically find success in integrating and living in lands where nature is respected, and power is earned rather than stolen or through bloodshed – often in lands where water is frequently found, and usually with cooler temperatures.

When you sleep in the night, it wraps around you.

You walk amidst the stars.

When you sleep in the day, you fall into it.

Let it catch you as you plunge.

Far, far away from your body.

Until the night comes to day or day comes to night.

Then the world ceases to be.

Ceases to be, for a time.

-Wollon Folk Song, Talon Flame

 

From the southern continent of Garrunga comes a people who once lived simple lives as hunter-gatherers. One day, the earth greatly shook and broke apart, and the air became acrid and stiff. The night remained in perpetuity. For a time, they did not know what caused this, until one known as Kuluru managed to walk in their dreams and come face to face with the beings of the sky at war with one another. He cast the spear to an Unduk-like being, where its two-faced body collapsed and bled through the sky, whereupon the night was given color, and a counterpart of day. The blood became shimmering and dancing auroras, and the platelets became the stars. From that moment on, the gangor knew of its beauty; as they slept, they would see dancing auroras and starlit nights that embraced them, and when they leapt into the Dreaming they fight to ensure such a beauty remains protected from those that would take it from them.

 

Linked By Heart and Mind

The Gangor are bipedal, marsupial humanoids with three dominant qualities that are exemplified by their lineage: their powerful legs, their prehensile tails, and their prominent ears. Once, they were a people considered separate, but over centuries their tribes, having met, fought, dined and slept in the Dreaming in face of the Unquenchable Shadow, they’ve unified and call themselves the Gangor, with shared history and heritage that spans just under a millennium. While the tribes do retain their cultural independence, they see another Gangor as brethren who share the same dream.

The general appearance of a gangor varies greatly by the traits of their lineage, but they bear an elongated muzzle, fur varying from shades of black to browns to white, pointed and long ears, strong or flexible prehensile tails, and powerful legs that are well adapted to jumping or climbing. For each of the lineages, one of these qualities ends up missing in some capacity. In some gangoran legends, the gangor once used to have identical appearances, but the war with the Unquenchable Shadows took its toll, and their peoples were cursed, splitting them into the three lineages known today.

An important aspect of the gangoran physiology is their sexual trimorphism. An individual can be born with male or female sexual organs, or a marsupial pouch that could carry and nurse young. In rarer cases, an individual can be born with a combination of these parts or none at all. While this may cause difficulties in certain stages of growth, medicine and nutrition can make up for the difference – both from modern discoveries and alchemy, or from traditional gangoran remedies and recipes.

 

A Desert of Magic

            The Gangor are natives from the continent of Garrunga, though some have found their way to the Isles of Mann long ago, potentially during the splitting of the supercontinent of Nugurua. Besides Zaho, Garrunga is potentially one of the oldest landmasses known in Ardor. Its location places it beyond the southern Margan Storms that has separated it from the mainland. With the Garrungan gangor finding their way back to the Ardorean mainland, the Mannish gangor have reunited with their long-lost, southern relatives. Since this event, the gangor have spread to much of the southern regions of Freke and Venteau.

            Garrunga itself is a land that shares similar, bizarre qualities to the Margan Storms just north off its coastlines. It thrives in natural beauty, though much of its mainland is a harsh desert with great mountains, and a prominent basin known as Hakar is a bountiful oasis that houses a primeval forest. During rains, the desert does flourish in a spectacular fashion for the briefest of periods, before it quickly recedes. Its coastlines feature prominent forests and jungles, and subarctic mountains that freeze during winter months.

            The gangor and its many, many tribes reside in all of these biomes, with at least 17 known major tribes scattered across the land. An important factoid about Garrunga – and informing the gangor as a whole is that much of this land is devoid of ether, and when ether is present, it is wild and unpredictable. A simple use of magic can bring unintended consequences if patterns to the etheric flow and its contents are not known; a fact that the earliest ether-bearing explorers in 989 MK were quick to discover – but a fact that is well-understood by the native gangor who have resided in the continent for centuries.

 

The Craftsmen of Heart and Soul

            While Ardor bathed in the discovery of magic and ethercraft, the gangor of Garrunga experienced such things differently, as did the gangor who settled in the Isles of Mann. The original legends of their people discovering the Dreaming, and their rituals of how to access it became the basis for many initial theories and excursions into the astral plane, which only became more understood as the Violet Phalanx drachiri began to enter academia to share their own people’s discoveries and color it through the lens of gangoran astral projection.

            Magic is a rarity, considered both a sacred gift and curse in many Garrungan tribes, where one must be careful in how it is used. As a result, many of these tribes are accustomed to using mundane weaponry and limited use of magic, and understanding that the wrong application of it could lead to sudden thunderstorms or explosions of fire. For that reason, their dependence on non-magical material opened them to a great understanding of mundane materials and their properties when they were brought by sleeping warriors into the dream or for waking warriors to fight in the physical world. Their understanding of physical chemistry at the time would impress alchemists, with knowledge of how to utilize incendiary materials, smoke and steam, or how to galvanize or smelt weapons with limited resources without terraforming their land to suit their needs.

But their physical homeland is what nourishes them and their bodies, to allow them to be prepared for sleep. Many tribes use magic sparingly, but much of this spellcraft is designed to prepare for their leap into the Dreaming, and their escape out of it. Whether it is the ritual components needed to enter it, or to assemble and empower charms, baubles, stones and weapons to assist in their astral journey.

            Most tribes have individuals with assigned roles in both the Waking World and in the Dreaming. In the Waking World, craftsmen often spend much of their efforts gathering and creating materials, traveling with hunters who would hunt for food or protect the craftsmen as they travel to places of power when the motions of magic would make conditions ideal for enchantment. The craftsmen then imbue their crafted objects with elements or facets that can be used by the warriors who enter the Dreaming. For example, when imbued with the powers of the storm, a well painted, carved gemstone would grant a dreaming warrior the power of lightning. A well-stitched tapestry with the patterns reminding a warrior of home blessed by spirits can lead the warrior home in the face of disaster. But not all crafts are specifically for the warriors; farmers and tenders often must contend with the whims of ether and spirits, and such charms can assist in placating or protecting their crop or their herd.

            But beyond these roles are the Seers. All garrungan and mannish gangor tribes have a seer, who works with their apprentices to ensure that no matter what happens, the souls of the warriors who sleep or their fellow tribesmen who die naturally or perish in their duties are safe from the eyes of the Terrors of Night. While specifics, terminology, and historical legends differ, they would cast their magic or entreat denizens of the Dreaming to help and protect their souls as the departed make their journey to join the wellspring of souls, known as the Aethronasth. For those who are not saved, the Terrors of Night would rend their souls asunder, cutting them off from the world forever. To those who could not be saved, they are called the Forgotten.

 

The Warriors of the Mind and Soul

The Dreaming is the layer that exists over the Waking World. From the earliest of gangoran legends, Kuluru discovered a war that was waged between its denizens, and with the cast of his spear, he chose a side for the Gangor to follow. As the Unduk-like beast bled and gave the blessing of the night sky and the auroras to their people, the gangor would take part in the Dreaming to protect it from the beings that threatened the Dreaming, for if they did not, the land would suffer and the dead would not rest.

Each tribe has a variant of the legends of the enemies that threaten the Dreaming, but they collectively become known as the Terrors of Night. In the Dreaming, they are monstrous creatures that eat away at the dreams of simple animals and plants, and gnaw at the magic residing in the earth. Should they be left unchecked, these animals and plants will turn hostile and sick, becoming cruel and wicked to all, and the magical pulses of the land will cease to be. Worse still, they feed on the souls of the dead and the spirits of the land, which cannot rejoin the flow of souls in the Aethronasth when they move on, and become Forgotten. While other denizens of the Dreaming fight against the Terrors of Night, the gangoran tribes send their warriors into the Dreaming to help.

As the warriors fight in the Dreaming, they keep the Waking World safer. Even so, warriors and hunters have their duties in keeping the physical world secure, as the after-effects of the conflict in the Dreaming can give rise to dangers that threaten their people. In the end, this unifying, two-front conflict, and the factors that are put into it, feeding into each other is why many gangoran tribes in Mann and in Garrunga have beliefs that are shamanistic or animistic.

 

Names to be Protected

            Gangor naming styles vary by tribe, and this is no different between Mannish gangor or Garrungan. A name could simply be a word that means something in their tribe’s native language. The Wollon tribe have names such as Bri, or Taka, or Dy; they do not have a familial name, though they would refer to themselves as members of the Wollon. But these names are often kept quiet or safe amongst members of the tribe, or among trusted people and allies. To many others, they would give a title they have been gifted from their successes to their tribe, and be guarded in giving their real name. These titles, such as Talon Flame, or Jack of Blades, hold a deep meaning of an individual’s accomplishment, but are safer to give. One must be wary in providing their true name, for one may not be aware the one asking is from the Terror of Night. The only time this can be comfortably shared is within the Dreaming, where the Terror cannot hide their true nature. Even so, some cautious and those slow to trust may still withhold their name.

 

A Bridge to the World

            The Gangor of the Isles of Mann were insular in the island nation, even before its unification. While known to many of the island tribes prior, they had remained distant on the isle of Kalobesi. They fought their wars in relative seclusion, until the arrival of Eirlanggan and Rogalian colonists that displaced them and placed their war in the Dreaming on hold. This had strong knock-on effects in the hold the Terrors of Night had in Mannish territories, that ultimately played a role in the outcome of the Mannish War for Independence. When General Aryanto unified the Mannish, he included the gangor of Kalobesi to repel the Rogalian colonists, and granted their tribes the island with three provinces in the newly founded Republic of the Isles of Mann. As a consequence of the war and their found place amongst a nation, the gangor had begun to set their eyes to other parts of the world as much as their own – and where else the Terrors might strike.

            Meanwhile, the Empty of Rogalia and Zahnheim were sent on boats to their death, far to the south in the Margan Storms. But as it so happened, the storms never touched their mundane boats and magic-less bodies, and eventually arrived on the continent of Garrunga. On their arrival, the Gangor were quick to foster them, and saw their lack of magic as more blessing than curse. With nothing on their persons, the Empty began to grow new communities. Though differences had led to conflicts, others had remained grateful to those who extended a helping hand – and they were dubbed by a different name, used to describe the Gangor who were born Empty – the sygican.

            As the sygican people settled, many grew their cities away from the tribes of the gangor, and their relationship was mixed, and in some instances strained. As the gangor shared their techniques and technology to the sygican, some had begun industrial and manufactory pursuits, which necessitated substantial changes and clearing of land. They had discovered how to use the incendiaries found to explosive effect, discovering substances dubbed gunpowder. Coal and steam could be used to power machinery that could automate resources. In the end, the sygican had become much greater proponents of archaeotechnology in Garrunga – technology that uses no magic. Eventually, they began to find ways to create boats that would insulate those with ether from the terrors of the Margan Storms, and reopen their journey northward.

            While some tribes had found the development that would threaten their land appalling, some could find the appeal as it made their lives safer and more reliable. The weaponry was an evolution of what their warriors were used to, but it also afforded them greater strength in the Dreaming. In this, the tribes are divided in how they would view the sygican as a whole. But when time came for the sygican to travel northward, to the lands that once shunned them, some garrungan gangor could not help but feel the pull to see what lay beyond the horizon. For some, it was adventure; but for others, it was the understanding that something had changed in how the flow of souls had behaved in the Aethronasth. For many of these gangor, they would eventually travel north – and reunite with their Mannish cousins, and discover the Lostfall that seemed to be responsible for the disturbances in the Aethronasth in the continent of Freke.

Gangor Lineages

The lineages of the gangor are determined by the sheer physical differences between their various forms, said to have been the result of their conflict with the Unquenchable Shadow. The Shadow was said to have cursed the gangor, removing one of their prominent natural gifts for each of the three lineages known today. Despite this, their ancestry shares much in the way of their origins, and sworn unification.

 

Heelock – The Dreamstriders

The Heelock traverse the great open plains and the desert. They have great, powerful legs that are capable of bending and stretching far, allowing them to have a pattern of saltation in their movements; they leap as they stride, moving across great distances, but they are cumbersome to use for shorter strides. Their tails are rigid and powerful, able to sustain their weight and help maintain their balance as they maneuver. They are the largest of the three gangoran lineages, with short fur meant for hotter climates and a tougher body. While their long, stiff ears can pick up sounds from great distances, they are not as powerful as the senses in other gangor.

 

Bilby – The Sharp-Eared Watchers

The Bilby are the shortest and smallest of the gangor, possessing soft, plush fur with frames that bear prominent, long ears that they have exceptional control over. Their ears can pick up on sounds and minute vibrations that alert them quickly to danger. Their legs can support powerful leaps and allow for substantial agility, though not as powerful or efficient as the heelock’s. Their tails, however, are short and do not possess the strong control that their other lineages have. Many bilby tribes have come from grassy plains and coastal hills.

 

Tenturun – Tillers of the Land

The tenturun are the gangor whose tribes thrived in the jungles of Mann and Garrunga. They have thick, coarse fur and rounded ears, some bearing prominent whiskers on their face. The fur keeps them relatively safe from insects and smaller parasites, and their tribes usually make it a point to keep it healthy and clean. Comparatively to the other gangor, their muzzle is shorter and rounded, and their legs are shorter and do not have the springiness that the heelock or bilby do. However, their claws are sharper and many tenturun tribes teach their young to climb trees, and make great use of their most powerful quality; their tail. Their tail is long and prehensile, covered in the same fur that protects their bodies, and function in many ways as an extra limb.

“In the depths they begin and end,

From the first drop of blood to the last,

For black rivers wind and wend,

The endless ring would wake the past.”

-From “The Elegy of Tria Solaidh”

 

 

The Origin of Darkness tells the creation myth of how the Aelkhazak came to be; a tale of when the first primeval beings who lived upon the world plucked the heart of The Serpent That Coils The World That Wakes, a mythical being that was said to wind around the universe. From the wound, black blood spilled. One drop firmly landed upon the base of the ocean, and this particular drop spread into eight rivulets. Each of these would lead to the birth of the Ana’zhak, who would then spawn their brood – the Aelkhazak. As their tale would say, the world they came to was full of life, and they lived in it as the sole inheritors of the land. As it bled from the wound, the blackened blood of the Serpent coated the deepest oceans and coated the seas around the Aelkhazak. The sands turned black and the world’s depths are coated in darkness – creating the Darksea.

 

A Slithering Form

The aelkhazak are an ancient race of amphibious serpentlike beings who have ruled much of Ardor’s oceans and northern continents for much of the age prior to the Awakening. Resembling snakes, they have a serpentine body with an upper torso, bearing a pair of forelimbs with the head of a snake. Their lower body is approximately two-thirds of their total body, with their upper-tail having musculature that would allow them to support their body upright or to foster the movements necessary to propel them forward on land or in water.

As a people, they once swam in the deepest depths of waters and in the darkest caverns of the world. Indeed, during the heights of the Aelkhazak Thalassocracy their grandest cities were submerged at the bottoms of the ocean floor, though such a capability has become a rarity in the millennia after their grandest cities fell and their people scattered.

Instead, as centuries passed and their people matured, their form began to evolve further with the snakes of the world. Notably, many had the ability to slither onto land or form feet through innate magic. Others adapted and changed with their inhabited waters and the lands. When the aelkhazak came across new inhabitants of the world, conflict shortly ensued. Through the centuries of fighting, their bodies became well suited for fighting on land or at sea.

Such tremendous diversity in their forms was attributed to the Ana’zhak, but ever since the fall of the Thalassocracy and the scattering of the aelkhazak across Ardor, such rapid evolution slowed. However, even in the face of the world they found themselves in, the serpents did not find their capabilities lacking, for they knew they were still lords of the water.

 


 

A Forgotten Origin

The Ana’zhak – a word that resembles anabranches to describe the branches of rivers – were said to be the originators of the aelkhazak today. Though their old poetry would speak of the eight Ana’zhak, collectively known as the Serpent’s Lyre, as kings and queens of their thalassocracy, they are far from royalty. Each of the Ana’zhak bears a desire and role said to have been seeded within them by The Serpent Who Coils The World That Wakes from the moment of the rivulet’s splitting. The Serpent’s Lyre consists of the following:

·         Aphos - Devourer of the Sun, whose brood are the Bringers of Change.

·         Levios - Guardian of the Sea, whose brood are the Watchers of the Dead.

·         Walli-Walli - Swimmer of Sleep, whose brood are the Bestowers of Boons.

·         Meirghul - Mistress of the Deep, whose brood are the Inscribers of the Void.

·         Tzalica - Hunter of the Sky, whose brood are the Treasurers of the World.

·         Garyu - Stalker of Falsehoods, whose brood are the Inflictors of Curses.

·         Vrathur - the Keeper of Creation, whose brood are the Followers of Hope.

·         Serulis - the Walker of Sands, whose brood are the Carriers of Knowledge.

 

The Ana’zhak are seen more as Gods and Creators, but not ones that are directly worshipped for divine power. Most aelkhazak of the time of their thalassocracy bore a pragmatism to the operations of their individual kingdoms, known as Tributaries, but many held a philosophical view of their origins and their place in the world at large.

Of those that did worship at the time of the thalassocracy, the aelkhazak prominently prayed to two entities. Some prayed to The Serpent That Coils The World That Wakes – represented by the Darksea, as an entity or place that the aelkhazak will eventually flow back to through the Serpent’s Lyre. In many ways, The Serpent and the Darksea are one and the same to the aelkhazak, where the most unfathomable depths of Ardor’s oceans are at the fringes of existence, where The Serpent has bled to create an unreachable, unimaginable shroud that carries occult secrets and power.

The other entity was known as the Black Sun. Ancient aelkhazak texts speak of Ixu’na’gaszh – the first city of their empire. This city’s foundation was built upon the ebon sands in Ardor’s depths, stained black by the droplets of The Serpent’s black blood. The droplet that spread into the eight rivulets of the Serpent’s Lyre formed a ring, that became the blueprint for Ixu’na’gaszh’s first walls. As the droplet congealed into cruor, it floated overhead as it refined and emblazoned itself into a five-pointed gem, shining in the depths with a dark, powerful and cryptic light. The Serpent’s Lyre proclaimed its name as the Black Sun. It is the emblem of the Thalassocracy as much as it was the crux of the empire’s occult supremacy in the world’s darkest depths. From within it, they claimed to have been able to interface with the Darksea, through each of its five points.

Scattered pieces of this scripture often spoke with their old world as one of dominance, utopia and endless knowledge that spanned beyond the known world, with some remnants of Ana’zhak books emphasizing certain elements over the other. The Book of Levios wove tales of their fallen city of Tria Solaidh which spoke of its beauty due to its location within fey-bound waters, while The Book of Aphos detailed the might of the empire in their fight against the divine watchers who saw the Ana’zhak as sacrilegious. Though it is scattered and incomplete, the components of The Book of Meirghul, salvaged by archaeologists, spoke of their pacts with Covenants with fallen empires beyond Ardor’s reach, in the deepest abysses of the Darksea.

 

The End of The Thalassocracy

As great as their Empire may have been, they were obscure to most in the wake of the Awakening due to a cataclysm that sealed their fate. When Mount Zaho erupted, the world entering the era of Meridae Kirosis changed violently and rapidly, and the Aelkhazak Empire was not spared.

Through salvaged scriptures or memory pearls, the accounts of those who lived through disaster spoke of a violent finale to an already declining empire. Even before Zaho’s eruption, the empire faced subterfuge and suspicion; they had cast out the Ana’zhak Meirghul for reasons known only to the Princes of the Tributaries, citing their overreach of the Black Sun’s power as betrayal. The Princes of each Tributary then began to slowly turn on each other, looking for traitors that had sent the Empire on their steady decline, or means of power to have their Tributary survive at the expense of others. Some began to fight over the right to the Black Sun.

By the time Mount Zaho erupted, most Tributaries had already ceded from the Empire as a whole in their spats amongst each other. However, the unthinkable happened in its wake. The Black Sun exploded, and so great was the cacophony and magic that was unraveled, the entirety of Ixu’na’gaszh and entire lands of the Thalassocracy were levelled, buried and destroyed. The Ana’zhak, who were said to have swum across the great city of Ixu’na’gaszh escaped from the city, and their broods and tributaries chased after them, while the Aelkhazak who were on the outskirts or survived the disaster scattered across the seas. Some eventually gave up on their effort and settled to make new Tributaries, while others vanished to seas unknown.

To this day, the Ana’zhak’s whereabouts are uncertain. Some Tributaries claim to bear them in secret, while others are said to have returned to the Darksea. From what is often revealed, these Tributaries still bear Princes who descended from the Ana’zhak, but little is spoken of their originators’ whereabouts. Even the younglings who are far more accustomed to life on land know or share precious little of the Serpent’s Lyre, save for the Princes who still serve them. To that end, they see the Ana’zhak in the same vein as an unseen deity or a covenantor; their powers are real, and often wielded by those who reach for their power. Whether it is truly the Ana’zhak who supplants this power or not is unknown.

 

Tributaries of the Modern Day

Despite the end of the old empire, the aelkhazak remain. From the darkest corners of Ardor to waterborne nations, one can find the rare aelkhazak. Many harbor exceptionally great desires to see their people restored to their former greatness, while others seek exclusion from their perceived enemies on land. Few have come to partner or assimilate with nations or people of other ancestries for the sake of their survival. Some had found success, while others have sought to prove or otherwise conquer their neighbors.

Some of these aelkhazak formed Tributaries, often associated with one or more of the Ana’zhak, but they quickly found that their people were in need of land-borne resources, such as elemental crystals or minerals. While some part of this was simply the price of progress, another fact was that some settled in waters far too barren to farm or too dangerous to hunt in. Through this scarcity and even a lack of working hands from the nature of the cataclysm that scattered them, some of these Tributaries are actively hostile against those on land.

For this reason, there are often tales told amongst sailors or sea and lakeside settlements to never dive too deep or swim too far. Certain waters are off-limits, lest one be taken into the depths by the aelkhazak to be turned to food or a watery ghoul servant at their beck and call. These particular Tributaries are not interested in conversation; they take what they can and kill who they must. Depending on their size, these aelkhazak groups are no political entity recognized by Ardorean nations, instead pegged as brigands or hostile forces that must be put down on sight. For those that are still hostile but open to discussion, some lakeside or seaside lands have taken to terse trade and an understanding of borders.

In a few instances, a Tributary has a substantial enough population and capability that was too difficult for a landborn nation to ignore. In a time as recent as 945 MK, the official proclamation of the return of the Tributary of Tria Solaidh was made by a Prince of Levios, who had reclaimed their homeland through the assistance of adventurers during the Second Age of Adventure. Though New Rogalia watches them warily, Tria Solaidh was keener on opportunities to let their newly formed nation flourish and sought trade and peace in place of war. By far contrast, since prior to the proper founding of the Empire of Eirlangga, a Prince of Aphos had sworn animosity to the worshippers of Dhusamat, which eventually evolved over centuries as a conflict to the nation that lasts to this day. At the edge of the crystalline Sarobi Cliffs is the eponymously named Tributary of Naga’s Vale, where amidst the glassy ruins of old khaitun settlements they fight tirelessly against Eirlanggan troops stationed to keep them at bay.

Much farther to the south is the Tributary of Basilisca, where Princes from both Levios and Aphos broods have sought their fortunes in North Rodda. They’ve created an enterprising thalassocracy of their own, where the term Tributary and Thalassocracy are interchangeable, and their homage to the Ana’zhak is split to differing neighborhoods. Through their actions in Rodda’s revolution, they have earned substantial power and fortune, becoming a naval powerhouse of Rodda’s northern coast – and profiting greatly due to their supremacy and position, despite any acts that border on piracy or black marketeering. Comparatively to other major aelkhazak settlements, Basilisca is far more interested in commerce, wealth, and local power than being directly hostile.

 

The Den of Princes

            Even after they had scattered and vanished, the Ana’zhak of the Lyre bears strong influences on cultures and viewpoints carried by the aelkhazak who have found homes elsewhere in the world. For a large proportion of aelkhazak-majority or exclusive Tributaries – which could be as small as settlements, tribes, or enclaves found in remote corners of Ardor, a council of Princes – also called a Lyre - would normally act as their leaders. At times different names are used in place of Prince, vaguely associated with a forgotten system of organization by size or purpose from the days when their empire still spilled outward from Ixu’na’gaszh. Whether these are still followed for cultural reasons or for a pining of what was lost is up to the individual. For the aelkhazak who manage to find themselves integrated in a settlement belonging to members of other ancestries, they frequently abide by local laws and rules, though some of their personal customs bring raised eyebrows.

            A Prince of an Ana’zhak is often seen more of an emissary or ruler, carrying a different meaning of modern usages of the word Prince and is irrespective of an aelkhazak’s gender. Depending on the size of their populace, they often work alongside multiple Princes to lead and act as a cultural guide to enforce their interpreted viewpoints and goals of their Ana’zhak.  In most instances, a Prince often is often a blood relative descendent to the Ana’zhak and bears a high station akin to nobility, while a Demi-Prince is a title reserved for a leader who shares no birth blood but circumstances demand they are best fit to lead. These Demi-Princes often already have a high station or title either in present or in the past during the time of the Thalassocracy.

            When leading, a Prince or Demi-Prince often espouses or leads according to the emphasized goals of their respective Ana’zhak. In the past, their directives were far more direct and firmer. Generations later, no tributary interprets their Ana’zhak’s goals in the same way. The Brood of Aphos and Levios are amongst the more prominent in mainland Ardor, and the Tributary of Tria Solaidh views the history of their loss as a mournful dirge and a hopeful return of a new generation, in line with Levios’ directives for the flows of life and death. But amongst the Zahoan kingdoms, the aelkhazak princes have emphasized the inevitability of death, aligning quite strongly to the fiends and hellish planes of Solum and Mortum. Such was their long-term plans to enact Levios’ penchant to be the keeper of the dead, that they have elevated one of their number, Tesh’Synark, to join the pantheon of Sophic Siblings.

            Not all Tributaries’ aelkhazak, even a Lyre’s princes are exclusively members of a single brood. While smaller representations of a particular Ana’zhak means that it is less likely that they would bear a Prince in the Lyre, some Tributaries attempt to have each Ana’zhak represented in some way, or give these Broods physical or cultural space in the Tributary. As a fallen and scattered people, such acts emphasize the one-ness and the unity their old thalassocracy once had for the aelkhazak as a people.

 

Honour in Names

Records of an Aelkhazak’s station, birth or blood are hard to come by given the sudden collapse of their old empire and the near millennia that has passed since. Even so, aelkhazak who perform admirably in their charge or their deeds frequently are bestowed honors to their lineage by aelkhazak Princes, which elevates their familial line.

            This honor often comes with the privilege of using a title as a prefix to an aelkhazak’s name. The title is sometimes the name of their own family, if their entire familial line is elevated; at other times it is a specific term in the aelkhazak tongue of khazakin to denote their achievement; but few honors come close than to share the family name of a Prince, typically aligning with a new station of service to them and their duties. Prior to such honor, an aelkhazak would only use their given name, as the use of a familial name or title is seen as an arrogant act. But just as this honor can be given, it can also be revoked due to shameful or destructive acts that put their Tributary or their brood at risk by the Prince who leads the brood an aelkhazak came from.

            The aelkhazak language of kazhakin is typically spoken and known amongst all aelkhazak, featuring syllables, hisses and consonants that both flow and gap with pauses and tremors that denote intent, tone and inclination. The tongue movements required renders it more easily spoken by reptilian ancestries of Ardor, though with difficult practice and phonetically adapted words other ancestries are capable of speaking it.
