The Draichsar were created by the Verum Drachiri at the peak of their ancient empire. Amongst the Drachenchild, they were once the cornerstone of the empire’s peoples, closest to the drachiri themselves, establishing architecture and arts as they served their creators dutifully. When the empire collapsed, the draichsar-kin spread across Ardor, though many stayed close to Drachiri patrons or matrons, as their eggs rarely hatch without the influence of arcane power, one more readily supplied by a dragon. But their intellect, ambition and power allowed them to find a home in numerous places in the world as they seem to have a knack for improving any field they apply themselves to.

 

Soaring, Flying Children of the Dragon

The draichsar could be described as bipedal draconic humanoids who bear wings upon their back. Their bodies are covered in scales and hide of a color that matches that of their draconic lineage, but much like their patrons or matrons of the phalanx of their ancestors, they bear numerous changes to their forms (albeit lesser ones) depending on the environments they have settled.

For example, the typical appearance of draichsar of the crimson scales appear as medium-sized, bipedal red dragons. But for the crimson phalanxes who migrated to the coarse mountains of Ulduur, they bear a more stony, sturdy appearance – one that matches the changes in appearance to the patrons and matrons that lead them there. However, they do not typically possess the rivulets and valves for molten blood and dracoleum as their phalanx’s drachiri would.

These changes are attributable to the magical nature of the drachiri, and subsequently the nature of the draichsar’s creation. In many ways, the environment’s ether flows and exchanges between a dragon and their chosen home, and as a result, it is often a shared reflection between the draconic inhabitants and their locales – a phenomenon not unlike spiritual domains’ effects on the material world, but in this instance, it is a purely material exchange.

 

A Magical Creation

The Draichsar-kin were made by the drachiri empire long ago to meet a need that the empire could not achieve with their other drachenchild; autonomous, unifying figures that could rally the other drachenchild and drachenfilli. They were hailed as the greatest creation of the empire, and the result of generations of magical experimentation between the Dominions of the Verdant and Ivory drachiri – two of the most magically and academically inclined dominions. The two dominions had worked to create drachenchild – many of the draconic creatures that are known to people today, but the draichsar-kin was the Verdant Dominion’s crowning work – coming at the price of great and terrifying experimentation on subjects, long-lost and forgotten to time in the drachiri empire’s apathetic view on mortalkind. This history is vaguely known amongst the draichsar themselves, and while some try to honor what went into their creation, others share in the apathy, if not at least see it as a worthy sacrifice to create them.

Even so, whether by design or by limitation, the draichsar-kin are born through magically infused eggs that are showered in draconic arcane magic. This magic can only come from a verum drachiri, a true dragon. Without it, the eggs simply will not incubate. In this way, though a draichsar-kin may lay eggs, they typically are still dependent on their patron or matron drachiri of their phalanx. In some instances, the draichsar must even pay tribute or a tithe (typically those from outside the drachiri’s phalanx) to a dragon to incubate them – typically an arrangement that sates the dragon’s Curse of Greed. For this dependence, some magical practitioners consider draichsar-kin a less-perfect attempt at creating a magical ancestry – seeing it as an attempt to recreate the wonder that gave rise to the lyncan. The only other magically created ancestry to be considered fully independent in this way were the vesperan – the crowning achievement of the Ivory Dominion.

Despite this, however, the magic that flows within the draichsar-kin is still powerful, and very much of a draconic nature. Magic comes freely to most draichsar, and it is almost as important to them as their blood. Magic is nigh-necessary to break through their etherically reinforced eggs by combusting their internal dracoleum to melt or destroy the eggshell. Shortly after hatching they very quickly learn or are taught how to channel their ether to maintain an internal cohesion. Without training, their magic can easily go awry when emotions run hot or when panic sets in. On the other end, Empty draichsar-kin almost always fail to break through their egg, and even if they do, they have an incredibly high mortality rate due to stunted growth or ill health, or an unintended combustion of their dracoleum results in internal damage.

 

A World With Wings and Scales

            Most draichsar-kin of today have little context of what their Empire is like, despite how many of them are often taught their history through the lens of the phalanx they grew up in. When the Drachiri Empire long ago was destroyed by the Great Beast Rahm, the remnants of the drachiri dominions scattered across Ardor. In many of these dominions, they employed Phalanxes, a collective of drachenchild and drachenfilli that are led by a single or pair of patron or matron verum drachiri for an established, singular purpose. These phalanxes fled; some went to isolation and hid themselves from the prying eyes of the world that they felt would hunt them down, while others swallowed their pride and dug their roots closer to the developing nations of the world. These phalanxes often bring with them their collective knowledge and history, which is then told and retold across generations of drachenchild and drachenfilli.

            The drachenchild include the draconically created creatures of the old empire – such as drakes (vrakin), pygmy dragons (skruli) and draichsar-kin, while the drachenfilli were subjects of the empire that were magically infused with dragon magic, to the point where their souls therianized to bear some of their draconic features. As generations would pass in these phalanxes, the faces of their communities would change over time depending on the patron or matron’s proclivities over time. Some phalanxes ceased to create or invite drachenfilli, while some could no longer control the drakes they raised. Others maintained it as best as possible, hopeful for the day the drachiri empire would rise again, or eventually, to give up and rule their own people. The drachiri would sire new draichsar-kin, but at times may leave the phalanx to find a partner to give rise to a new brood of dragons. If they would die, perhaps their child would take over. Or perhaps, the child would abscond, or raze what the patron had worked so hard to build. In the process, the draichsar would need to find their own way; and for many, survival and bearing new whelps would mean to find a drachiri patron or matron to swear allegiance to – or to serve indentured.

            Not all outcomes are as bleak, but survival as a drachiri phalanx is often difficult. For the phalanxes that have found success, they might have an assured territory of their own, far away from the prying eyes of mankind or their nations’ geopolitical boundaries. The drachiri guard their land jealously with the assistance of their phalanx, and in some instances have menaced or created agreements with far-reaching townships for a continued tribute in return for safety against other threats or for minerals that their nests would bear – typically to alleviate their dragon’s Curse of Greed. These phalanxes understand a one-way relationship between an unrazed township and a phalanx is a quick way to ensure a group of powerful people would be sent to end the life of their dragon matron, typically for the chance to raid their hoard.

            In another instance, the drachiri phalanx finds themselves firmly planted in the dealings or the day-to-day of a nation. Some nations, such as Varenzia, strongly revere the drachiri’s penchant and grasp of magic. They were among the first countries to welcome dragons and work alongside them to develop their nation, and have been quick to formalize agreements to secure each other’s safety from other nations – which could also include other dragons who may eye their territory. Other nations such as Shizuchiro in the continent of Akai or Hualai in South Rodda actively revere the dragons that have settled in their countries, and are said to now be led by them due to their past history and skill in successfully maintaining their Dominion. Others famously have a spiritual kinship with dragonkind, such as the nation of Krymmenos in North Rodda. There, the dragon Safira had given her life to protect the people in the wake of the downfall of the Eirlanggan Empire, and to this day many of its peoples continue to try and achieve the same lofty ideals she had. While the Phalanx she led has been disbanded, the descendant draichsar-kin still find themselves welcome amongst their townsfolk, even if they must seek other dragons elsewhere to incubate their eggs.

 

A Distant Curse

An inevitable part of a phalanx led by a verum drachiri is the Curse of Greed that each of the six scales of dragon bears. The nature of each curse is different for each scale, but each dragon feels a strong need to amass representations of their greed to feel accomplished; if left ignored, the curse manifests into an uncontrollable emotion that threatens to overtake them. The emotion is powerful; crippling at best, or devastating at worst. This threat is what typically defines the way how a dragon perceives the world and how they might rule their phalanx in an era after the six dominions of the drachiri empire. This is typically why most agreements with independent phalanxes are rarely straightforward, fair or kind, and why dragons often demand tribute or tithes for a continued, comfortable existence. Without satiating the curse, a dragon quickly loses much of their control.

This inevitably leads to a trickling sense of responsibility to draichsar-kin who serve a drachiri patron or matron. Their phalanxial duties often serve their needs in some way, or act in service to it. Fortunately in their case, the Curse of Greed does not seem to pass onto the draichsar-kin or any other drachenchild or drachenfilli, at least not at the same extreme. Some might feel the tug or sway of the Curse of Greed for Pride to exert themselves and prove themselves above all their peers or feel deeply unsatisfied. Others might be greatly materialistic, seeking Wealth at all costs. Some of this might be cultural, however, and the line is sometimes very hard to discern.

These cases are still apparent, even among draichsar-kin who have chosen to live outside the boundaries of a phalanx and persist amongst people of other ancestries. They find themselves trying to excel at the roles they apply themselves to or indulge in vices quite readily compared to some others, but none could deny the zest and zeal they act upon the things that they are deeply infatuated with. If nothing else, a suspiciously wealthy draichsar could fund an entire livelihood in a village, but they could be acquiring their wealth from either an impressive business or a very well-thought out racketeering scheme. These qualities have made draichsar-kin pretty apt leaders, bureaucrats and merchants, even if they can be overzealous for one’s tastes.

 

Magic, Flowing Free

            In the end, these qualities and their natural reserve and dependence of magic have integrated many draichsar into the daily workings of anywhere they flap their wings into. As magic cycles between them and their environment, they harbor potent magical capabilities if they choose to develop it. Those that do frequently become prominent practitioners, able to effortlessly use their reserves to combine, channel, and cycle ether. In this way they are naturally-born scions of magic, spontaneously casting spells without needing to do excessive preparation or study. After all, from the very beginning of their hatching, they often learn to use their arcane-infused organs to breathe fire. As they age, they might be able to focus on energies that are more intrinsic to their scaled lineage.

            This does not make them slouches in other applications of magic. If anything, draich-sar possess a combination of traits that make them powerful warriors as much as they can sling spells. With their wings, they can easily maintain their flight much more rapidly compared to other winged ancestries, and fight readily while flying. The spontaneous magics allow them to swoop, dive and perform imbued strikes with their weapons readily. If there was any doubt these draichsar were created by the Empire with war in mind, these capabilities can easily shatter it.

Cazic-fer

            When a soul has been so inundated in the hellish powers that swirl in the Zaho, their bodies begin to show changes. First, there could be tufts of soft fur. Next, they may find a protrusion of bone growing from their skulls one morning. Their children might be born with horns. Eventually, they could bear hooves. For some, these changes might come incrementally; but for those who are showered in the frenetic magics of the azoph-fer, replete with the confluence of Zaho’s cosmic and spiritual energies, the transformation of the soul and body is violent – and often bloody.

            Cazic-fer is the name given to those who have been soulmorphed by the influences of the powers that suffuse the realm of Zaho. While this is often attributed to Azoph-met’s divine essence, other great spirits create and affect the domain as well. This includes not only the fiendish and war-forged divine spirits that influence Zaho, but also those of Azoph-met’s siblings such as Ezmodun. Most cazic-fer are soulmorphed azoph-fer due to the nature of their creation and the land they are originated from, but in rarer cases people of other races have undergone this transformation or passed these traits to their children.

            The cazic-fer often bear various bovid-like features, with cloven hooves, furred bodies with horns or antlers on their head. In some more benign cases, the transformation is only partial and leaves some part of the original ancestry’s features intact. More often than not however, the transformation is complete to the point where unless one were to learn the power to temporarily shift back, it is a permanent change. The most common cazic-fer resemble goats due to Azoph-met’s image, but rarely forms of bulls, moose, sheep and deer can be found, due to the other siblings of Azoph-met.

 

Playing a Cazic-fer

Your soul is strongly influenced by one of the Sophic Siblings, or one of the great divine spirits residing in one of the Hells or Zaho. You gain bovid or fiendish features such as horns, a forked tongue, long or short tufted tails, or might bear cloven hooves for feet, or completely appear as a bovid humanoid closest in affiliation to these forces.

 

You gain the Cazic-fer and Fiend trait. You gain low-light vision, or you gain darkvision if your ancestry already has low-light vision. You can select Cazic-fer feats and feats from your ancestry whenever you gain an ancestry feat. Finally, you gain the Cazic-fer Shapeshift heritage action.

 

Cazic-fer Shapeshift (1A)

Traits Concentrate, Polymorph

You change away from your cazic-fer form back into your ancestral form or return to your cazic-fer form. While in your ancestral form, you look like your original ancestry, but might bear a tell-tail sign that you have such planar influences upon you.

Draich

The draich are those who are influenced by the powers that spill forth from dragons, gaining draconic qualities that resemble their benefactors. Amongst the drachenfilli of the Drachiri Empire, the draich were once those considered trustworthy or useful enough to be granted a dragon’s power. In the era after the empire’s fall, the drachiri spread across Ardor, and whether through romance, servitude, bargains or an overwhelming exposure to draconic magics from a dragon’s death, more draich therians are created.

Many draich have minor external features that resemble their draconic benefactors, such as scales growing on parts of their body, or formations of draconic ridges or horns. They might possess scintillating eyes that could resemble that of one of their benefactor’s dominions, or even sprout a very stunted dragon’s tail. In some cases, these influences are greatly pronounced and a person is transformed or born with entire physical limbs that resemble a hybrid between man and dragon, or sprout leathery dragon wings not unlike that of the draichsar.

Worldwide, the draich are indicators of where a dragon has been present. In some cultures such a thing is a gift, while in others it is a curse. Many draich are sometimes accused of trading parts of themselves or acting as spies for dragons who scheme and plot to overtake their towns, while others are elevated to be leaders who bear a great deal of magical or martial gifts from greater beings. While the truth varies from place to place, draich who manifest much of their draconic lineage bear powers that harken to the source of their therianization. Fortunately, the Curse of Greed that the drachiri bear do not manifest in the draich, nor does it appear in a reduced form like it would for other dragonkind, but some cultures find this connection and gift to the dragons fair reason to emulate their benefactors.

While the process of becoming a draich is unique to those who are not draichsar, a draichsar is still not immune to the inundation of draconic power from a patron or matron in their phalanx. For them, they attain great power that only exemplifies their own natural gifts. In truth, any draich – be it another ancestry or a draichsar – have an immense power that they must learn to tap into as they become closer to a dragon, which is a bastion of magical power that is so strongly tied to the material world.

 

Playing a Draich

You bear draconic influences in your soul. You might have minor physical influences but your inner magic works similarly to a drachiri benefactor, or you might have substantial changes to your morphology and reflect the bloodline or magical form that has imprinted into your soul. You gain the Dragon and Draich trait, and you can select Draich ancestry feats. You choose a Drachiri Benefactor from the table in the Draichsar ancestry and one trait from that benefactor’s Elements & Energies column, but no other benefits. If you have a Benefactor from another source, you can choose another trait you do not have if they are the same Benefactor.

 

In addition, you gain access to the Drachaic language and gain a +1 circumstance bonus to Diplomacy checks to Request or Make an Impression with draconic, spiritual or elemental denizens who are affiliated with domains or environments that align with your Benefactor’s Domains, Aspects & Themes, and you can make Diplomacy checks with them even if you do not speak their language.

The intent for Lineages is to allow for greater diversity within the umbrella of an ancestry. In Ardor, the Sapien, the Loupain, the Azoph-fer and many other ancestries have a diverse variety of body types and shapes, histories of being inundated with magic, inherited powers, and more. Lineages allow a degree of expression within an ancestry that pertains to their physiology and allows a greater design space without having to separate them out into a new ancestry, or limiting them to a heritage.

 

Creating a new ancestry has some mechanical and thematical implications. Mechanically, an ancestry is distinct enough from another to where overlap is not possible without a certain way to cross it over (such as with the Adopted Ancestry), and has the expectation of a full progression of feats for all levels. Thematically, it implies that these ancestries have very strong, distinctive histories, cultures and identities that is shared between members within it, and is not shared with members outside of it. In certain cases, this may be true. In the future, if Ardorean ancestries are fleshed out in such a way that necessitates a lineage to be designated as an ancestry, that path will be considered.

 

On the other hand, heritages as designed function more as an indicator to a character’s more regional and ancestral origin, and is too narrow to depict what is essentially a sub-classification within an ancestry (even though certain Golarion ancestries use it in this way). Similarly, concepts of Ethnicities and Nationalities are elements that fit within a character’s immediate upbringing and their place of birth; both of which are covered in Backgrounds but otherwise confer no other additional benefit. In short – Lineages fit a design niche but also allow to paint a greater picture of an ancestry, while heritages remain as a display of geographical and cultural influences within that ancestry.

Certain character options, such as the Cleric class, offers a selection of Domains for a character to be associated with. In most instances, in Seekers of Ardor a Domain is aligned with a deity, or a greater spirit that exudes enough of a presence. A domain is used in certain character options where Clerics gain Domain Spells based on the domains of their deity, but it can also grant certain effects to certain feats. The new Domain Boon feat for Clerics allows them to grant a boon associated with their Domain.
